10000-the-magna-carta:
This file gathers the texts of Magna Carta, the Great Charter that King John granted in 1215. The charter opens in John's voice, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine.

It sets out the liberties granted to church, barons, and freemen. Several versions are included, some corrected by volunteers after rough transit, with a Latin version promised. Readers can compare the charter's famous clauses on justice, taxation, and due process. It remains the starting point for anyone studying English liberty and the rule of law.
10006-la-fiammetta:
Giovanni Boccaccio's La Fiammetta, here translated by James C. Brogan in 1907, is an elegy in prose from a lady in love to other ladies. Fiammetta writes because her woes, felt rather than eased by time, have grown greater, and she longs to win pity by telling her sorrows.

Her tale follows love's rise, betrayal, and long ache, told with the frank feeling that made Boccaccio famous. Addressed to noble ladies whose love may be more fortunate, the book speaks across centuries about jealousy and longing. Readers get an early masterpiece of psychological fiction, in a clear modern translation.
10649-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-14:
John Lord died in 1894 before he could finish his Beacon Lights of History, so this fourteenth volume was added by recent writers as a supplement. It surveys broad achievements of the last fifty years, the period Lord himself never reached. The publishers admit no single volume could cover so much in Lord's vivid, personal manner.

Instead, the writers follow his method where they can, treating great movements through leading figures and turning points. The volume rounds out the series for readers who want the story carried toward their own time. It works as a capstone to a popular history that had guided general readers for years.
11255-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This volume of Slave Narratives gathers interviews with formerly enslaved people in Arkansas, recorded by the Federal Writers' Project between 1936 and 1938 and assembled by the Library of Congress. Informants speak in their own words about work, family, punishment, freedom, and life after emancipation. Names run from Silas Abbott to hundreds of others across the state, with photographs illustrating the text.

Because the interviews came decades after slavery, they mix sharp memory with the caution of elderly speakers talking to white interviewers in the Jim Crow South. That tension is part of their historical value. The volume remains a firsthand source for the daily experience of slavery, told by those who lived it.
11422-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This volume of Slave Narratives, part seven of the Arkansas narratives, gathers Federal Writers' Project interviews from 1936 to 1938, assembled by the Library of Congress and published in Washington in 1941. Informants run alphabetically from Charlie and Ellen Vaden through Nettie Van Buren, the Wadilles, the Walkers, the Washingtons, the Watsons. the Williamses, and on to Yates, each telling of slavery, freedom, and life after emancipation in their own words.

Like other Arkansas parts, this volume mixes memory, dialect transcription, and interviewer framing, requiring careful reading. Its alphabetical arrangement makes it a reference work as well as a narrative collection. Historians value it for the range of voices it preserves from a single state.
11485-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This Kansas volume of Slave Narratives, prepared by the Federal Writers' Project and assembled by the Library of Congress in 1941. is unusually brief, with only three informants: Clayton Holbert, Bill Simms, and Belle Williams. Holbert, eighty-six, born and raised in Linn County, Tennessee, tells interviewer Leta Gray of Pleasant Holbert's plantation of about one hundred slaves. field work during the Civil War's end, and a father, brother, and uncle who fought for the Union.

Holbert describes homespun clothing, looms, yarn socks, and hog killings of fifteen to a hundred animals, with corn, barley, and cotton raised for subsistence. The volume's thinness reflects Kansas's small formerly-enslaved population interviewed there. Its value lies in Holbert's detailed, first-person account of Tennessee plantation life.
11544-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Federal Writers' Project workers interviewed former slaves in Arkansas from 1936 to 1938. The Library of Congress gathered the typed records in 1941. This part, the fifth for Arkansas, names many informants in order. Charlie McClendon and Lizzie McCloud lead the list, with Avalena McConico and Ike McCoy nearby.

The Millers, Moores, and Morgans follow among the names, through to Perry Madden and Lewis Mann. Each account is in the speaker's own words. They cover work, food, family, punishment, and freedom as remembered late in life. Read together, the narratives give a ground-level record of slavery and its aftermath in Arkansas.
11552-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Federal Writers' Project workers interviewed former slaves in Maryland from 1936 to 1938, and the Library of Congress gathered the typed records in 1941. This eighth volume names informants from Lucy Brooks and Charles Coles through Page Harris, Silas Jackson, and Rezin Williams, with interviewers' names reconstructed where stamps were cut off.

One account recalls wool clothes in winter, cotton in summer, and Sunday clothes given at Christmas, with shoes likewise. A marriage on the farm in 1863 was repeated by a Baptist preacher in 1870, since the first was not legal. Another tells of an owner and overseer who carried whips together. The interviews keep Maryland slavery in first-person memory.
11691-driftwood-spars-the-stories-of-a-m:
Captain Percival Christopher Wren wrote Driftwood Spars in 1912, with stories of a man, a boy, a woman, and others who strangely meet upon the sea of life. The epigraph, from Matthew Arnold, compares men to driftwood spars that meet and pass on a boundless ocean plain.

Part one follows John Robin Ross-Ellison's early life, part two Moussa Isa Somali, and part three a woman with Augustus Grabble, General Murger, and others. A later scene brings a general inspecting fusiliers and a civilian who answered a dinner invitation rudely. The book links far lives by chance meetings.
11709-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Federal Writers' Project workers interviewed former slaves in Arkansas between 1936 and 1938, and the Library of Congress gathered the typed records in 1941. This sixth part for Arkansas names informants from Doc Quinn and Henrietta Ralls through the Robinsons, Rogers, and Rosses.

Frances Smith, aged seventy-seven and living in Pine Bluff, recalls seeing Yankees in Mississippi and remembering little of her old master beyond his name, Spencer Bailey. She says what little she remembered she has forgotten, and did not try to keep it up. The interviews preserve slavery in plain, late-life memory, state by state.
11920-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume 7 of Slave Narratives, covering Kentucky, gathers interviews with formerly enslaved people recorded by the Federal Writers' Project between 1936 and 1938 and assembled by the Library of Congress in 1941. The typewritten records preserve the speakers' own words, including dialect spellings, as they recall slavery, freedom, and life afterward.

Narrators describe being sold at auction, where traders tested strength and size, and one man recalls nineteen years and nine months in bondage. Preachers' sermons on hellfire appear alongside memories of family separation, giving the volume its force as testimony: history told by those who lived it, rather than summarized by others.
12028-the-uttermost-farthing-a-savant-s-:
R. Austin Freeman's The Uttermost Farthing, subtitled A Savant's Vendetta, opens with a narrator who admits misgivings about making public a strange history communicated by a lamented friend. Contents run from The Motive Force and Number One through The Housemaid's Followers, The Gifts of Chance, and By-products of Industry to The Trail of the Serpent.

Freeman, known for his scientific detective Dr. Thorndyke, here lets a man of science pursue revenge with methodical patience, using knowledge as a weapon. The novel's interest lies in its cold, reasoned villainy: a vendetta planned like an experiment, carried to the last farthing. Told by a witness who only slowly grasps what he has heard.
12055-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume 9 of Slave Narratives, covering Mississippi, gathers interviews with formerly enslaved people. They were recorded by the Federal Writers' Project between 1936 and 1938 and assembled by the Library of Congress in 1941, illustrated with photographs. Informants include Jim Allen, Anna Baker, John Cameron, Gus Clark, and many others, whose names open the volume.

Mississippi narratives recall wakes where mourners clapped hands, kept time with feet, and chanted all night in a practice called Walking Egypt. They also recall charms against bad luck, such as throwing salt in the fire and a broom across the door at the cry of a shivering owl. The volume preserves speech, belief, and memory from the Deep South, in the speakers' own words.
12297-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This volume of Slave Narratives, assembled by the Library of Congress from Federal Writers Project interviews of 1936 to 1938, holds Florida narratives. Typewritten records, prepared under the Works Progress Administration, preserve the words of former slaves interviewed in old age.

Informants recall work, punishment, family separation, and the coming of freedom, with stories like Delhia mother told that she would soon be as free as her master. Interviewers sometimes shaped the talk, and modern editions note their biases, but the voices remain direct and irreplaceable. The volume is a primary source for American slavery and emancipation, told by those who lived it, in their own phrasing and memory.
12430-a-lecture-on-physical-development-:
S. R. Calthrop of Bridgeport, Connecticut, delivered this lecture on physical development and its relations to mental and spiritual development before the American Institute of Instruction at Norwich on August 20, 1858. Ticknor and Fields published it in 1859, after five thousand copies were voted.

The lecture links bodily health, exercise, and habit to mind and spirit, and calls on schools to train the body as well as the intellect. A mid-book fancy pictures an extempore volcano shooting a listener up through the earth crust into the very hole he had been digging. The lecture is earnest mid-Victorian physiology, mixing science with moral uplift. It shows how educators then linked gymnastics, diet, and character.
13217-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume twelve gives the Ohio narratives of Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States. It was prepared by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936 to 1938 and published at Washington in 1941. It gathers typewritten interviews with former slaves, assembled by the Library of Congress and illustrated with photographs. Informants include Charles Anderson, Melissa Barden, Susan Bledsoe, and many more.

Speakers recall slave weddings read from a book by master or mistress, games of Hulgul with hazelnuts in cabins, and funerals never seen. One word picture describes Thomas McMillan of Steubenville, five foot six, 155 pounds, who collects junk by hand cart and reads his Bible. The volume is a vital oral record, in the speakers' own words, of slavery and freedom in Ohio.
13579-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Slave Narratives, volume five, Indiana narratives, gathers interviews with former slaves prepared by the Federal Writers' Project between 1936 and 1938 and assembled by the Library of Congress in 1941. Informants include George W. Arnold, Rosa Barber, Mittie Blakeley, Julia Bowman, and many others, with photographs throughout.

Jane bewitched chickens until a great fire burned the charm and no more died, Mrs. Colbert laughs over family memories in a comfortable home, and William, given a horse and six months' rations after abolition, starts a new life. Charles and Lydia French send for girls to go to school in Cincinnati in 1867, where no Kentucky schools then existed. The volume preserves voices of slavery and freedom in the speakers' own words.
13602-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume four of the Federal Writers' Project slave narratives, assembled by the Library of Congress and printed in Washington in 1941. Presents interviews with former slaves in Georgia, recorded between 1936 and 1938. The speakers tell their own stories in their own speech, as taken down by project workers.

They recall work in the fields and houses, food and housing, overseers and punishment, family ties, and the coming of freedom. Some remember kind masters and some remember harsh ones, and the accounts often differ in tone from one speaker to the next. The value lies in firsthand memory: voices that history books had left out, speaking plainly about bondage and its end.
13700-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume two, part two, of the Federal Writers' Project slave narratives, printed in Washington in 1941, gathers interviews with former slaves in Arkansas, recorded between 1936 and 1938. The speakers, listed by name at the front, recall their lives under slavery and after emancipation in their own words.

They speak of masters both kind and cruel, Christmas holidays on the plantation, work, food, and the Ku Klux Klan, and of later moves by rail to new homes in Arkansas. One man says his people were better off under a kind master than free after his death, a view the collection prints without comment. The interviews stand as raw oral history, uneven and personal, and all the more valuable for it.
1374-vendetta:
Balzac's Corsican tale opens in Paris in 1800, where a foreigner, his wife, and a small girl stand before the ruins of a house. The family fled Corsica under a blood feud, and the daughter, Ginevra, grows up torn between her father's code of vengeance and her love for a young French painter.

In a Paris studio, Ginevra's choice brings the old feud into a new city, and the tale moves toward a grim, fated close. Balzac sets Corsican honour against French city life with stern clarity. It is a short tragedy of family duty, love, and revenge that admits no middle way.
13806-overland-through-asia-pictures-of-:
Thomas W. Knox travelled overland through Siberia, China, and Tartary in the 1860s and wrote this large illustrated account. He crossed Kamchatka and Siberia by sledge, river, and horse, then went on through Mongolia and China. Nearly two hundred illustrations show costumes, dogs, sledges, and town life. A map helps readers follow the route.

Knox describes tea drinking, the fur trade, bear hunting, and Siberian dogs with lively detail. He notes Polish exiles, Russian officers, and native peoples along the way. Hard travel, cold, and strange food fill many pages. The book captures Asia just before railways changed it. It remains a rich source for travel history and for daily life in Siberia.
13847-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This volume gathers slave narratives from interviews with former slaves, prepared by the Federal Writers' Project between 1936 and 1938. The Library of Congress assembled the typewritten records in Washington in 1941. Project files, correspondence, and memoranda explain how interviewers worked and how editors judged the material. The District of Columbia project forms the focus here.

Former slaves speak in their own words about bondage, work, family, and freedom. The narratives preserve dialect, memory, and detail lost in formal histories. Editors' notes warn readers about interview conditions and selection. The volume serves historians, students, and general readers alike. It stands as a vital first-hand record of American slavery.
1432-seraphita:
Balzac's mystical novel follows Seraphita, a being of strange beauty and double nature, loved by both a man and a woman in a remote Norwegian valley. Neither lover can fully grasp Seraphita, whose talk of angels, Swedenborg, and the life of the spirit lifts the tale beyond ordinary romance.

Dedicated to Madame Hanska, the book is Balzac's boldest venture into mysticism, blending philosophy with a love story that ends in transfiguration. Its prose is rapt and strange. Readers seeking Balzac the realist may be startled; those open to his spiritual side will find a singular work.
15348-blown-to-bits-or-the-lonely-man-of:
R. M. Ballantyne's 1894 tale of the Malay Archipelago, Blown to Bits, takes its spark from Krakatoa's violent eruption in 1883. A preface praises the beauty of eastern seas, the wide reach of the eruption's phenomena, and the devastation that followed. A frontispiece shows a hero coming on a cavern.

The lonely man of Rakata, an island near the blast, faces volcano, sea, and survival, with Ballantyne's usual adventure vigor. Illustrations by the author add drama. Boys' adventure readers will find the book thrilling, vivid, and rooted in a real natural disaster.
15606-the-life-of-the-truly-eminent-and-:
M. de Burigny wrote this life of Hugo Grotius in French, published in London in 1754 for A. Millar and others in the Strand and Fleet Street. Its title promises a copious history of the important and honorable negotiations in which Grotius was employed, together with a critical account of his works. Burigny's preface wishes Grotius had found a historian equal to his fame.

Earlier lives, Burigny says, gave only a surface account and a catalogue of works, neglecting the two most interesting distinctions of Grotius's life: his negotiations and his sentiments in religion. Book one follows his origin, the marriage of Cornelius Cornets with Ermengarda de Groot, his birth, boyhood hopes, and an embassy to Henry IV of France. The biography is long, learned, and old-fashioned, a monument to a jurist, diplomat, and theologian.
15725-don-a-perfecta:
Benito Perez Galdos wrote Dona Perfecta, here in an edition with introduction and notes by A. R. Marsh and vocabulary by Steven T. Byington, from the Athenaeum Press, Ginn and Company, Boston, Cambridge, Massachusetts, March 1897. A new impression conformed accentuation to the fourteenth edition of the Academy's Dictionary, corrected misprints, and added a vocabulary. Notes that merely duplicated the vocabulary were dropped.

New notes, found while compiling the vocabulary, shed fresh light on passages where old notes stood, so the shorter notes hold more information than before. Notes gloss Spanish words and allusions: a word for sent down, a term like Diana, a coachman like Phaethon, and Mercury as god of commerce. The edition serves students reading Galdos in Spanish: a classic novel of a provincial town, a young engineer, and a formidable aunt, with full scholarly apparatus.
16195-a-sketch-of-the-history-of-oneonta:
Dudley M. Campbell's 1883 sketch traces Oneonta, New York, from its Native past to a settled town on the upper Susquehanna. Before the Revolution, the valley saw bloody contests between Indian tribes for its possession, with Delawares long at home on the river and Tuscaroras pressing up from Chesapeake Bay. Settlements at Otego Creek and Charlotte mouth left orchards and tools behind, until Sullivan's troops destroyed them in 1779.

German Palatine families from Schoharie and the Mohawk became the first settlers, felling forest and raising homes where German was the common tongue. Later merchants like Jacob Dietz, who arrived about 1804, built stores and estates at the town's center. The sketch offers a compact, readable local history for readers of New York's frontier past.
16204-the-mansion-of-mystery-being-a-cer:
Chester K. Steele's 1911 detective novel, from the International Fiction Library in Cleveland, opens with a young man in a tremendous hurry. The moment his ferry bumps into the slip he dashes ashore. He hails a taxicab and orders the driver to the Vanderslip Building with all possible speed. He sinks among the cushions with his handsome face wrinkled by care. A chapter called The Story of a Double Tragedy sets the case.

Steele, author of The Disappearance of John Darr, builds his mystery from haste, money, and a mansion with secrets. Investigators, suspects, and sudden turns keep the reader guessing in popular-novel style. Fans of early American detective fiction will enjoy its pace and its cliff-hanging openings.
17700-the-suppression-of-the-african-sla:
W. E. B. Du Bois wrote this monograph on the suppression of the African slave trade to the United States. It runs from 1638 to 1870, as volume one of Harvard Historical Studies. It was published in New York in 1896 by Longmans, Green, and Company. Chapters open with an introduction and the rise of the English slave trade, then the planting colonies and their restrictions.

Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, and Maryland each get their restrictions weighed, with the general character of those restrictions summed up. Later chapters follow the trade through debate, bargain, and suppression. Readers get Du Bois's doctoral study, the foundation of modern scholarship on the slave trade.
18051-hilda-a-story-of-calcutta:
Sarah Jeanette Duncan wrote Hilda, a Story of Calcutta, in 1898, put out in New York by Frederick A. Stokes. Duncan, author of A Social Departure and A Daughter of To-day, sets her tale among the English in India, where actresses, officers, and society folk cross paths.

The book opens with Miss Howe, an actress, pushing a portière aside with a curved hand, her gown crying luxury with the cheapest voice. She bends over Laura Filbert on a bamboo sofa, and the social comedy begins. Duncan writes with sharp wit and a keen eye for Anglo-Indian life. It is a bright, period novel of Calcutta society.
18484-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume four, part three, of Slave Narratives presents Georgia narratives from interviews with former slaves. The Federal Writers' Project prepared them in 1936 to 1938. The Library of Congress project assembled them, and Washington published the volume in 1941 with photographs. The volume gives typewritten records of people who had lived under slavery, in their own words as interviewers set them down.

Informants in this part include Jennie Kendricks, Emmaline Kilpatrick, Frances Kimbrough, Charlie King, Nicey Kinney, Julia Larken, George Lewis, Mirriam McCommons, and Ed McCree, among others. Each narrative tells a life: work, family, masters, freedom, and memory. Readers get American history from those who bore it: first-person testimony, plain and direct, preserved before the last witnesses passed.
18485-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
The Federal Writers' Project prepared this volume of Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States from interviews with former slaves. The Library of Congress project assembled it, and it was published in Washington in 1941. This is volume four, Georgia narratives, part four, distinct from part three elsewhere in this slice.

The informants list opens with names from Telfair, Georgia, and the interviews give first-person memories of slavery, work, family, and freedom, recorded in the 1930s. The volume stands as a direct record of voices that would soon be lost. The Works Progress Administration preserved it for readers and historians.
18869-on-limitations-to-the-use-of-some-:
J. W. Powell, director of the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology, wrote this paper on the limits of anthropologic data. He warns that the mass of published archaeology has often been put to unwise uses, above all in linking North American tribes to ancient peoples of other continents.

Camp and village sites, graves, mounds, and ruins, he argues, can show how art grew in savage and barbaric life and hint at customs, but they cannot carry grand claims of kinship. Man was already widely scattered by the quaternary period, and all known American sites belong to the present epoch, long after the original dispersion. Until the first home of mankind and the earth's old geography are known, migration lines cannot be drawn with sense.
18912-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
The Federal Writers' Project prepared these typewritten records between 1936 and 1938, assembled by the Library of Congress and published in Washington in 1941. This volume, the fourteenth, presents South Carolina narratives, part one, from interviews with former slaves. The project was sponsored by the Library of Congress under the Works Progress Administration.

Each narrative preserves one person's memories of slavery, work, family, and freedom, in the speaker's own words and speech patterns. Together they form a folk history unmatched in directness. Readers get firsthand testimony of American slavery and emancipation, essential for understanding the period from those who lived it, and a landmark of oral history.
19264-japanese-literature-including-sele:
Epiphanius Wilson compiled this revised 1900 volume, Japanese Literature, with Genji Monogatari and classical poetry and drama, plus critical and biographical sketches. Chapters follow the Chamber of Kiri, the Broom-like Tree, Beautiful Cicada, Evening Glory, and Young Violet. The aim is to open Japan's court literature to English readers.

Wilson notes Genji as a partly political work, written in pure classical Japanese before military rule and feudalism changed the land for seven centuries. Court life, poetry, and romance fill the selections. Readers get a pioneering anthology of Japanese classics, dated in places yet still inviting.
19294-the-outdoor-girls-on-pine-island-o:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this Outdoor Girls tale about Pine Island and a cave and what it contained. Betty, Amy, Grace, and Mollie return to Deepdale after a spring of diamonds, kidnapping, and rescue, then set out on a joyous ride that nearly ends in a crash. The series was sold at fifty cents a volume.

Frank's car loses its brake, bolts out of control, and plows half its length into a haystack. The girls, buried in hay, laugh once fear passes. Readers get a lively girls' adventure of motors, caves, and friendship on Pine Island.
19397-history-of-rationalism-embracing-a:
John F. Hurst wrote this history of rationalism and Protestant theology, published by a New York firm in the late eighteen sixties in a revised third edition. It surveys how reason came to test scripture, creed, and church teaching, with an appendix listing the literature of the debate.

Hurst follows small circles of ministers and laymen, pastoral conferences, and church assemblies as they faced new dangers to old faith. Though written from a churchman's view, the book remains a useful map of a century of doubt, argument, and attempted repair. An early chapter follows George Calixtus and Jacob Boehme through the disputes that came right after the Reformation.
19446-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This volume gathers slave narratives collected as a folk history of slavery in the United States, drawn from Library of Congress manuscripts. Formerly enslaved people tell, in their own words, how they first heard of freedom, often at a table where a brother brought the news over supper.

Families left old homes, moved to new states, and rebuilt lives after bondage, and their accounts carry the plain detail of work, faith, and loss. The volume is a primary source of great weight, preserving voices that history books once passed over in silence.
19610-selections-from-previous-works-wit:
Samuel Butler gathered these selections from his earlier works, with remarks on G. J. Romanes and his book on mental evolution in animals, plus a Psalm of Montreal, published in London in the mid eighteen eighties. The preface opens a sharp scholarly quarrel.

Butler charges Romanes with claiming that Canon Kingsley wrote on instinct in Nature in early eighteen sixty-seven, years before Nature began to appear. The volume shows Butler the polemicist: witty, exact, and eager to catch a rival in a factual slip. One selection warns that words draw hard lines where none exist, splitting man, ape, and monkey by name alone.
19764-the-moccasin-ranch-a-story-of-dako:
Hamlin Garland called The Moccasin Ranch a story of Dakota, and dated it 1909. Its Dakota is cold, wet, and hard: ice-ridged fields, swales full of water. Geese fight the wind overhead while ducks sit on ice-rimmed ponds. The sod lies burned black and bare, firm with frost. A wagon rattles noisily over that frozen ground.

Garland built his name on honest tales of farm hardship. He rejected pretty lies about pioneer life. Dakota settlers in his work face debt, weather, and loneliness. The ranch of the title concentrates those pressures. Readers get realism from a man who lived the life. This tale is Garland in his true country.
19932-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Slave Narratives gathers first-person accounts of American slavery, a folk history in the tellers' own words. One woman remembers a morning her mother was gone. She woke, went to her mother's room, and found her missing. She cried and cried for her, she says. Her mistress would not let her leave the house to search. The fear was she would try to find her mother. Such separations haunt narrative after narrative here.

The Federal Writers' Project interviewed elderly survivors in the 1930s. Their dialect was written down as spoken, however imperfectly. Thousands of pages record work, family, faith, and cruelty. No other source lets the enslaved describe slavery so fully. These volumes anchor American memory of the institution. Every page is testimony, not literature alone.
20222-an-ethical-problem-or-sidelights-u:
An Ethical Problem weighs experiments on men and animals in science. Its subtitle calls it sidelights upon such work, pro and con. Public feeling on vivisection is confused, the book says at once. No agreed definition of the word itself has yet been fixed.

That lack of a shared term muddles every debate on the subject. The book sets out phases of animal experiment one by one. It asks where knowledge ends and cruelty begins in the lab. Readers get a sober, early map of a fight that still runs hot today.
20524-culm-rock-the-story-of-a-year-what:
Glance Gaylord's Culm Rock tells the story of a year in a boy's life on a barren shore. Culm Rock is a point of rock and sand where the sea is never silent. It would have been an island but for narrow strips of sand heaped high like ridges.

That slender bridge binds the rock to the mainland. Often it seems the hungry sea will tear the bridge away. In that lonely place, the year brings the boy loss, work, and faith. The story belongs to the religious tales once given to children as Sunday reading.
20785-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
A man born in Louisiana ten years before the Civil War tells his tale in his own words. He recalls the war's start with a child's clear memory. His voice is one of many in Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States.

In the 1930s, field workers wrote down the memories of the last living ex-slaves. Work, food, faith, cruelty, and freedom fill their plain, strong talk. These accounts form a key source for American history, told from below. No reader can meet these voices and keep a thin view of the slave past.
21268-the-search-for-the-silver-city-a-t:
James Otis set this tale of adventure in Yucatan, published in New York in 1893. The region was then almost as unknown as the interior of Africa. His introduction quotes E. G. Squier on the blank map between Chiapas, Tabasco, Yucatan, and Guatemala, where the Usumacinta River gathers a thousand tributaries. Maya peoples who resisted Spain still sheltered there.

Young Neal, pictured wrestling a great reptile, joins the search for a fabled silver city in that fastness. Jungles, plains, pine plateaus, and hidden ruins fill the road. Otis wrote many boys' adventure books, and this one mixes real Central American geography with a treasure hunt.
21508-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Former slaves tell their own lives in the South Carolina narratives, part two, gathered in the late 1930s. Federal Writers' Project staff typed the interviews from 1936 to 1938. The Library of Congress issued the set in 1941 as a folk history of slavery.

One woman tells how her mother was free before the war, so she herself was never enslaved. Others recall farm work, town hotels, masters, and kin lost or kept. The editors kept each speaker's own spelling and turns of phrase. These plain voices form a record no outside history could supply, and they demand slow, heedful reading.
21640-a-bid-for-fortune-or-dr-nikola-s-v:
Guy Boothby's Dr Nikola returns in A Bid for Fortune, or Dr Nikola's Vendetta, reissued in 1918. A restaurant manager on the Thames Embankment opens the prologue in a state of dread. Nikola's letter and a fine repeater watch, at half-past seven, mark the hour of crisis.

The narrator's holiday in Sydney turns into a chase through London and Port Said. Imprisonment, escape, and a free passage granted by Nikola himself follow. Lord Beckenham's tale and a trail through the islands close the hunt. Boothby's master villain, cool and ruthless, made the Nikola tales a sensation of their day.
21764-child-stories-from-the-masters-bei:
Great poems and works of art become simple tales for children in Maud Menefee's Child Stories from the Masters. The book appeared at the turn of the century. Menefee had told stories to the same circle of children for years, and drew on the great books when she needed fresh material. She does not retell full plots, which lie beyond a child's reach. Instead she takes a scene, a stanza, or a single purpose from each work.

Pippa passes into spinning and weaving games, while Siegfried and Parsifal arrive as knight tales with their music. Millet's Spinner fronts the book. Menefee hoped teachers would use her method with their own classes. She wanted children brought close to poetry and art early, through story and handwork together.
21781-text-book-of-biology-part-1-verteb:
Backboned animals are the subject of this textbook of biology, part one of two, devoted to the vertebrates. The book was later reworked by A. M. Davies in 1898 as a textbook of zoology, then revised again by J. T. Cunningham. This text keeps the first and second editions, with dissections redrawn by Miss A. Robbins. It was built for students learning animal structure at the bench.

Chapters teach through dissection, with labeled plates and careful terms for each part. The transcriber fitted the text for voice readers, hoping blind students and children could use it too. As a period schoolbook, it shows how biology was taught when the knife and the drawing, not the screen, trained the eye.
22166-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
In the 1930s the Federal Writers' Project sent interviewers across the South to record former slaves. Their typescripts, assembled by the Library of Congress, form the Slave Narratives. This volume holds life stories told in the speakers' own words. Elisha, an old man, tells his interviewer he foresaw her coming to write down his memories.

Narrators recall sale, labour, hunger, kindness, cruelty, and freedom's arrival. Their speech is kept in dialect spelling, which modern readers handle with care. Taken together, the interviews are the largest body of testimony from the enslaved themselves. Historians lean on them heavily. Few books in this library carry voices of such direct witness to slavery.
22976-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Louisa Adams introduces herself in these Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States. My name is Louisa Adams, she says. I was born in Rockingham, Richmond County, North Carolina, and was eight years old when the Yankees came through. She belonged to Master Tom, her mother was Easter, her father Jacob, and she names her brothers and sisters in order.

Thousands of such interviews were gathered in the 1930s from the last living Americans born enslaved. Work, family, punishment, food, and freedom fill their pages in the speakers' own words. No history of slavery carries their weight of witness. The dialect spellings belong to the interviewers' practice of the time, and readers should hear the voices through them, not past them.
24006-shadows-of-shasta:
Joaquin Miller, author of Songs of the Sierras and The Danites in the Sierras, published Shadows of Shasta in Chicago in 1881, dedicating it to Whitelaw Reid. Its introduction asks why this book, and answers with a sight from the previous year, in the heart of the Sierras.

Miller saw chained women and children marched from cool, healthy Sierra homes toward degradation and death on the reservation. Bayonets kept the chained line in order, and beside it rode a young officer bright in gold and brass, fresh from the charity school on the Hudson. Their fathers and brothers had died in battle on mountain heights and in lava beds. Miller's book, with chapters on Mount Shasta, man-hunters, and an escape, is a protest against that march.
24108-fables-in-rhyme-for-little-folks-f:
W. T. Larned adapted these fables from the French of La Fontaine into light verse for children, with pictures by John Rae. In a preface for parents, Larned calls La Fontaine's fables the most entertaining ever written, yet notes that prose versions lose the soul that made them classics. He offers rhyme instead, so young readers can taste something of the original wit and blithe spirit.

Some fables keep closely to the French text, while others drop political, mythological, and literary allusions too hard for a child. The book is addressed to little Americans, hoping they grow better acquainted with their French friends. Readers get short animal fables in verse, made for reading aloud.
2473-mary-gusta:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Mary Gusta follows a Cape Cod girl who grows from a shy child into a woman of strength, holding her family and town together through hardship. The novel's heroine faces loss, love, and the sea's dangers with quiet courage, while Lincoln's dialect and humor warm every page. Mary Gusta herself is the book's heart.

The story is gentle and episodic, built from the rhythms of small-town life. Readers who like Lincoln's Cape Cod world will find a favorite. It is a tender, old-fashioned novel. Lincoln set the novel in a Cape Cod town much like his own Chatham.
24827-rita:
Laura E. Richards published Rita in Boston in 1900, in her Margaret series, with pictures by Etheldred B. Barry. Rita Montfort, dagger in hand, is a girl of spirit, and the story carries her into the world of the Spanish-American War. Richards tells readers that its boldest scenes match published accounts of that war.

A night scene shows a camp roused by whispered alarm. The Gringos are here, and soldiers snatch arms from beds of moss and leaves while a general and his officers buckle on sword belts. The tale mixes girls' adventure with war romance. Young readers will find a brave heroine and a stirring, if old-fashioned, picture of war.
25154-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Slave Narratives, volume two, Arkansas narratives, part four, gathers interviews with formerly enslaved people. They were collected by the Federal Writers' Project between 1936 and 1938 and assembled by the Library of Congress in 1941. This part covers informants whose surnames run from Jackson through Johnson.

In their own words, men and women recall slavery, work, family, and freedom, including the coming of Grant's army, rejoicing at emancipation, and the hard years after. Some speak of pensions, farming, and prices in old age. The volume preserves voices that would otherwise be lost, and it remains a central source for the history of American slavery.
25794-indian-legends-of-minnesota:
Mrs. Cordenio A. Severance compiles Indian Legends of Minnesota, published by D. D. Merrill in New York and St. Paul in 1893, with Minnehaha as frontispiece. She dedicates the volume to Mrs. Francis B. Clarke and Mr. Delos A. Montfort, whose inspiration and help made the undertaking possible.

An epigraph in verse tells a darker vision of a nation scattered, forgetful of council, weakened and warring, sweeping westward like cloud rack and withered leaves. Contents open with The Lone War-path, and legends that follow preserve Minnesota Native stories, heroes, and places in a form meant for general readers and schools.
25994-a-refutation-of-the-charges-made-a:
Rev. Horace Edwin Hayden answers a charge from Benson J. Lossing's history of the Civil War in this 1879 pamphlet from Richmond. Lossing had written that explosive and poisoned bullets, found on the Gettysburg field, were sent by the Confederates, and had pictured them as the most fiendish of missiles. Hayden sets out to refute the claim that the Confederate states authorized such balls.

His evidence turns to Union ordnance records, not Confederate ones. In May 1862, Gardiner offered explosive musket shells to the United States government, and President Lincoln asked General Ripley, chief of ordnance, whether the shell would serve in battle. Ripley replied it had no value as a service projectile. Hayden argues the charge rests on error, not on proof.
26192-a-handbook-of-the-cornish-language:
Henry Jenner's 1904 handbook, issued by David Nutt in London, teaches the Cornish language in its latest stages, with a history of its literature. Jenner, a member of the Gorsedd of the Bards of Brittany, opens with seven known Celtic languages and their place in the Indo-European family, beside Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, and the Teutonic tongues.

Later pages trace Cornish through its decline, when English creed and prayers first reached parishes that had used Cornish beyond memory. The book quotes old petitions and writers such as Carew and Borlase. It serves both as a grammar for learners and as a plea for a tongue that had nearly slipped from daily speech.
28170-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Slave Narratives, volume fourteen, South Carolina narratives, part four, Washington, 1941, gathers interviews with former slaves made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936 to 1938. The Library of Congress assembled the typewritten records, with photographs, under the Works Progress Administration. Informants include Mary Raines, Frank Range, Sam Rawls, and many others, from Raines to Starke.

Each narrative tells, in the speaker's own dialect words, of bondage, work, family, freedom, and life after emancipation. Spelling and grammar quirks are kept, save for plain printer's errors. The volume stands as a vital primary record of American slavery, told by those who lived it.
28973-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
This volume gathers Virginia narratives from Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States, drawn from interviews with former slaves. Typewritten records prepared by the Federal Writers' Project from 1936 to 1938 were assembled by the Library of Congress and published in 1941. The Virginia volume lists informants from Fannie Berry of Petersburg to Mary Jane Wilson.

Fannie Berry's interview, taken by Susie Byrd in February 1937, opens with her mistress crying that the enslaved people were rising, a memory Berry links to Nat Turner's insurrection. The narratives preserve voices, spelling, and memory as the interviewers heard them. Readers get primary testimony about American slavery, recorded in the speakers' own words before that generation passed.
29727-zero-data:
Charles Saphro's short tale follows Jason, a cop in the fall of 2009, hunting guilt he cannot pin on Lonnie Raichi, a fabulous, irreproachable philanthropist. All the intricate electronic witchery of the twenty-first century cannot catch Lonnie. Jason sweats it out, seeking a fourth, final, all-knowing rule to smash Lonnie's triple ethic. Lonnie, small, heavily built, wet-eyed, and dapper, credits all his success to his philosophy.

Jason commands more and more men, with new techniques from Gov-Pol and Gov-Mil labs, yet gets less and less help from his superiors. Saphro builds a tale of law, philosophy, and a cop's disgust. Fans of science-fiction crime will enjoy a sharp, brainy story of rules, ethics, and pursuit.
30090-robinetta:
Kate Douglas Wiggin tells how Robinetta Loring, a pretty American widow of twenty-two, seeks a home in England after her host falls ill. Maria Spalding, who took Robinetta in for a London season, must leave for Nauheim on doctor's orders, leaving her guest stranded with few friends. Maria writes to Augusta de Tracy at Stoke Revel, begging her to receive the girl, whose mother Cynthia ran away with an American years before.

Robinetta longs to see Stoke Revel, the picture she was named after, and Lizzie Prettyman, her mother's old nurse across the river at Wittisham. Augusta de Tracy, widow of an admiral and guardian of a young grandson, reads the pleading letter in a shabby Victorian room full of family photographs. Wiggin's comedy turns on that clash: English pride, American warmth, and a promise to a dead mother.
3022-a-cumberland-vendetta:
John Fox Junior wrote A Cumberland Vendetta as a novel of feuding families in the Kentucky mountains. The story opens with two hunters stepping from a cave that served as childhood hiding place. A tall mountaineer carries a Winchester, and a boy carries a squirrel rifle longer than himself, now seeking refuge against hunger or darkness. They climb from rhododendron thickets to a mountain shoulder above a river.

The feud between the Stetsons and Lewallens shapes every meeting, while a girl's startled eyes and talk of Isom out of his head show how violence unsettles the young. Fox writes mountain speech with care and sympathy. The novel remains a classic of Appalachian fiction, tense in its hunting scenes and tender in its love story.
30224-a-prairie-infanta:
Eva Wilder Brodhead sets a novel in a little Colorado mining town, opening with Miss Jane Combs in the doorway of her broad, rough, paintless shack on a May morning. Jane built the house after her own ideals on a treeless street, and the single street of the town stretches before her as the story begins. Pictures reproduced by courtesy of The Youth's Companion show a doctor scowling over his glasses as he listens.

Henry Altemus published the Philadelphia volume in 1904. Its six chapters run from the power of consolation and a sacred charge to a true benefactress, wise impulses, destiny pressing, and bewildering satisfaction. Captions hint at the wider cast: Lolita, a lady of fortune called Tia, and Tesuque, the rain god. The novel blends prairie life with warmth, duty, and sudden turns of fate.
30576-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States, gathers interviews preserved from the Library of Congress Manuscript Division, with inconsistent punctuation silently corrected and clear spelling mistakes fixed. Inconsistent language use, such as day and dey, is kept, and a list of corrections closes the book.

Numbers heading each interview were stamped on the originals and point to the interview's place in the whole Slave Narratives project. Two handwritten notes are retained and annotated as such. The volume gives first-person testimony in the speakers' own words, a vital record of enslavement, survival, and memory for readers and historians. These voices speak plainly, and their words still move readers today.
30622-the-unknown-quantity-a-book-of-rom:
Henry Van Dyke writes The Unknown Quantity, a book of romance and some half-told tales, copyrighted in 1912 and published in New York in October 1912 by Charles Scribner's Sons. Reprints ran through July 1921, with a leather edition from 1913. Van Dyke takes his epigraph from Legendre's Algebra: let X represent the unknown quantity.

The book is dedicated in thankfulness to the memory of his daughter Dorothea, ray of light, song of joy, heart of love, 1888 to 1912. It opens with a poem on deeper crimson in the rose and deeper blue in sky and sea. Van Dyke blends romance, loss, and faith into tales where the unknown shapes human lives.
30967-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Held here is volume sixteen, part two, of the Texas narratives in Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States from interviews with former slaves. The typewritten records were prepared by the Federal Writers' Project from 1936 to 1938, assembled by the Library of Congress Project of the Works Progress Administration. They were issued at Washington in 1941, with photographs. This volume was prepared by the Federal Writers' Project for the State of Texas.

Its informants include Willis Easter, Anderson and Minerva Edwards, Ann J. Edwards, Mary Kincheon Edwards, Lucinda Elder, John Ellis, and Lorenza Ezell, among many others. The interviews keep the speakers' own language, with inconsistent spellings of names and places left as given. It is a vital primary source: former slaves telling, in their own words, what slavery, freedom, and life after emancipation meant to them.
31219-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Volume eleven, part two of Slave Narratives was prepared by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936 to 1938 and assembled by the Library of Congress in 1941. It preserves interviews with formerly enslaved people in North Carolina. Its informant list runs from John H. Jackson and Ben Johnson through the Jones, Lassiter, Lawson, and Lee families to the Mansons, Moores, Parkers, Perrys, and Ransomes, with dozens more.

Each narrative gives a formerly enslaved person's own account of bondage, work, family, and freedom, typewritten and illustrated with photographs. As folk history, the volume lets readers hear slavery's survivors in their own words, county by county, before that generation passed.
31277-anglo-saxon-grammar-and-exercise-b:
C. Alphonso Smith's Anglo-Saxon grammar and exercise book, dated 1896, teaches Old English in three parts. Part one introduces the language's history, sounds, inflections, word order, and practical suggestions for learners. Part two works through etymology and syntax: the a-, o-, i-, and u-declensions, strong and weak verbs, pronouns, adjectives, numerals, and comparison.

Part three offers selections for reading in prose and verse, with line notes and a glossary, so students can move from paradigms to real texts. Systematic and classroom-tested, the book served generations of students meeting Beowulf's language for the first time.
31535-a-monk-of-cruta:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's A Monk of Cruta, published by the J. S. Ogilvie Publishing Company of New York with copyright in 1894, is a novel of mystery and romance. Its contents list chapters with evocative titles: "The Black-Robed Phantom, 'Death,'" "The New Art," "The Dancing Girl," "Adrea's Diary," "The Far-Off Muttering of the Storm to Come," and "An Ashen Grey Delight." Oppenheim, author of The Peer and the Woman and A Millionaire of Yesterday, builds the story around a monk, a phantom, and a woman's diary.

The novel belongs to Oppenheim's early period, before he became famous for thrillers of diplomacy and crime. Its atmosphere is Gothic and romantic, with a monastery, a dancing girl, and a gathering storm. Readers of Victorian popular fiction will find a curious, atmospheric tale, where mystery and sentiment share the stage.
32895-a-veldt-vendetta:
Bertram Mitford's novel is told by Kenrick Holt, a reserved young man who admits he has no friend in the world at the time his story begins. Working at a dull, sedentary job and living among mere acquaintances, he sets out on a voyage of discovery that carries him to southern Africa. There, old quarrels, fierce loyalties, and the open veldt reshape a life that had seemed narrow and stuck.

The vendetta of the title grows out of that new country, where personal wrongs are settled under harsher rules than Holt knew at home. Mitford fills the tale with frontier travel, strong characters, and the tension between English reserve and African violence. It is a colonial adventure of its period, driven by one man's slow change from watcher to actor in a feud not of his making.
33002-the-shoemaker-s-apron-a-second-boo:
Parker Fillmore's Shoemaker's Apron retells twenty Czechoslovak fairy tales and folk tales in English, with illustrations and decorations by Jan Matulka. Drawn from original sources and chosen for variety, the stories include gorgeous Slavic fairy tales and small nursery tales fit for telling anywhere. Folk tales show the wit of a canny people, and rollicking devil tales surprise an Anglo-Saxon reader as much as they entertain. Fillmore calls them vivid renditions, not academic translations.

Fillmore was both a student of folklore and a storyteller in his own right. The tales keep that double life: faithful to their sources, yet told with pace and voice. Shoemakers, devils, kings, and clever peasants crowd the pages, and the collection works well read aloud. It remains a lively door into Czechoslovak folk imagination, gathered at a time when that young country's tales were still fresh to English readers.
33659-mammals-of-northwestern-south-dako:
Kenneth W. Andersen and J. Knox Jones Jr. survey the mammals of northwestern South Dakota. The survey appears in this 1971 University of Kansas Museum of Natural History paper, volume nineteen, number five, pages 361 to 393, with eight figures. The mammal life of the western Dakotas and adjacent Montana was relatively poorly known, and no earlier report had studied a restricted area in detail. The authors summarize information from Harding County, where more than fifty species are known to occur.

Harding County covers about 2,700 square miles of the Missouri Plateau's Cretaceous Table Lands, organized in 1881 with present boundaries fixed in 1908. Rolling hills and flats of short grass and sage, broken by buttes rising four to six hundred feet, shape its mammal life. The report gives naturalists and land managers a detailed baseline for a Northern Great Plains fauna.
34002-dick-s-desertion-a-boy-s-adventure:
Marjorie L. C. Pickthall wrote this tale of early Ontario settlement, published at Toronto in 1905 with seven pictures. Dick, a boy in Canadian forests, faces the fall of a tree, a day in the woods, a backwoods Christmas, and the call of the forest. A message from a wanderer, a prairie journey, and a storm in the grip test him.

Stephanie, to whom Dick returns, anchors the story, and a goodly heritage closes it. Pickthall writes of woods, snow, and family bonds in a golden early fall. The book remains a warm adventure tale for young readers.
34036-the-story-of-malta:
Maturin M. Ballou wrote this history and travel book on Malta, published in Boston and New York in 1893 by Houghton, Mifflin. Ballou, author of books on Alaska, Cuba, and round-the-world travel, turns here to an island long fought over in the middle of the sea. The volume traces Malta's past and present for American readers.

Ballou writes as a traveler-historian, mixing story, description, and notes on places worth seeing. The book serves readers who want Malta's sieges, knights, and harbors in one readable volume. It remains a pleasant nineteenth-century guide to the island.
3486-the-inca-of-perusalem-an-almost-his:
George Bernard Shaw writes a short comic play about a ruler Shaw calls the Inca of Perusalem. The figure is a thinly veiled portrait of the German Kaiser during the First World War. Shaw explains that he wrote it while the Kaiser was still a powerful foe, not a fallen prisoner. He added obvious fiction to free himself from the duties of sober history. Fear of the man, Shaw says, made some readers angry that he was not afraid of him.

The playlet treats the emperor as a man who knows better than his own legend, and it mocks court flattery and military pride. Shaw's comedy works by deflating a dreaded enemy into a human figure. Readers who enjoy Shaw's wartime satire will find a brief, teasing piece rather than a history lesson.
3673-essays-before-a-sonata:
Charles Ives writes essays to accompany his Concord Sonata, a piano work honoring American thinkers. The contents run from a prologue through essays on Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts, and Thoreau, to an epilogue. A biographical sketch notes Ives's years from 1874 to 1954 and his place as a bold American composer.

Ives writes about music as thought, praising Emerson's freedom, Hawthorne's shadow, and Thoreau's closeness to nature. His prose, like his music, breaks rules, with sudden turns and plain American speech. The book suits readers interested in American music and in the Transcendental writers who inspired one of its most original composers.
6009-the-valley-of-vision-a-book-of-roma:
Henry Van Dyke takes his title from a friend's question: can one see farther from a valley than from a mountain top? He answers that the mountain gives outlook over earth and sea, while the deepest visions of life's meaning come in the valley of suffering, endurance, and self-sacrifice.

Van Dyke reads the outcome of the Twentieth Century War as a victory over the mad illusion of world dominion glimpsed from Germany's military peak in 1914. He dedicates the book to his children and their children, who may recall these troublous times. Romance and half-told tales carry his reflections.
703-lucasta:
Richard Lovelace wrote these lyrics to Lucasta, his beloved, and to friends, war, and love itself, in the age of the English Civil War. Songs, sonnets, and odes praise a lady's eyes and hair, bid farewell to soldiers bound for the wars, and jest about love's power. The best known lines send a lover off to battle with honour intact.

Lovelace was a Cavalier poet, writing from prison and exile as his cause failed. His verse is graceful, witty, and at times sad, with a courtly ease that hides real loss. The volume gathers the poems that made his name, and it remains the classic set of Cavalier lyrics: love and loyalty sung in short, musical lines.
7299-obiter-dicta:
Augustine Birrell's Obiter Dicta takes its title from law, where an obiter dictum is a gratuitous opinion, an individual impertinence that binds none, not even the lips that utter it. Birrell's preface to the American edition calls it a very little book to introduce to so large a continent. Yet he found the notion of being read in America most fragrant and delightful when Scribner proposed the edition on honourable terms.

The essays that follow are talk in print: opinions offered lightly, with wit and learning, and left free for the reader to take or leave. Birrell writes as a man of letters at ease with books and company. The volume charms by its modesty, claiming nothing more than a passing remark well made.
7355-texas-a-brief-account-of-the-origin:
This brief account of Texas, extracted from a larger geographical, statistical, and historical work then nearly ready for the press, appeared in 1836. Some numbers had first printed in the New Orleans Bee and Bulletin. Its preface admits the title promises more than the pamphlet holds. As war is now the order of the day, only a small portion of the political part of the Texas work is presented here.

The author hopes enough is unfolded to show the origin, progress, and present state of the colonial settlements, with an exposition of the causes that induced the existing war with Mexico. The pamphlet thus reads as a hurried wartime sketch, not a finished history. Its value lies in its moment, Texas at the edge of revolution.
7446-the-naturalist-in-la-plata:
W. H. Hudson, joint author of Argentine Ornithology, spent years watching the animals of the La Plata region of South America, and this book sifts what he learned. His plan was to keep only facts that seemed worth recording about the habits of the animals he knew best. Linked subjects are grouped under one heading where his thoughts led him that way. Illustrations by J. Smit accompany the third edition of 1895.

Bird life gets only a fair share here, since Hudson had treated it at length in his larger work. The rest ranges over mammals, insects, and the strange behaviors of pampas creatures, all observed at first hand. An index at the end makes good the contents list's gaps. It is a classic of South American natural history, written by a man who lived among his subjects.
8442-europe-and-the-faith-sine-auctorita:
Hilaire Belloc argues in Europe and the Faith that Europe is the faith, and the faith is Europe, with the Latin motto, without authority there is no life, on the title page. Contents move from what the Roman Empire was, through what the church was in the empire, the fall, the beginning of nations, Britain, the Dark Ages, the Middle Ages, and the Reformation.

Belloc, a Catholic historian and polemicist, writes history as argument: the Reformation was not progress but a wound, and Britain's defection from Rome broke Europe's unity. Readers, whether they agree or not, meet a forceful, readable thesis that shaped Catholic historiography. The book remains a classic of confessional history, provocative by design.
8543-the-great-north-western-conspiracy-:
Winslow Ayer, a physician, wrote The Great North-Western Conspiracy in all its startling details. It tells of a Civil War plot to plunder and burn Chicago, release rebel prisoners, seize arsenals, and raid from Canada. The subtitle promises the plot to burn New York, piracy on the lakes, parts for the Sons of Liberty, the trial of Chicago conspirators, and inside views of their temples.

Ayer writes as a contemporary exposé, naming names and describing secret societies. Readers get a sensational, partisan account of wartime conspiracy in the Northwest, from a Union loyalist. The book interests Civil War historians for its picture of Copperhead plotting, and readers of conspiracy literature for its breathless detail.
901-the-jew-of-malta:
Christopher Marlowe wrote this tragedy of Barabas, the rich Jew of Malta, who loses his wealth to the island's rulers and plots revenge without mercy. Played before king and queen at Whitehall, the play follows Barabas through murder, poison, and treachery, as Turks and Christians fight for Malta itself.

Marlowe gives Barabas a fierce, witty voice, part villain and part victim of bigotry, and the play's energy never flags. Edited by Alexander Dyce, this text preserves the famous tragedy in full. The Jew of Malta remains a landmark of Elizabethan drama, bold, bloody, and darkly comic.
a-bid-for-fortune-or-dr-nikola-s-vendett:
A Bid for Fortune, or Dr Nikola's Vendetta, is an 1895 thriller by Guy Boothby, and the book that introduced Dr Nikola. Nikola may be the world's first modern supervillain: a master of hypnotism and mind control, a telepathic adept, and a skilled astral projectionist. He can make ordinary men see images in pools of liquid and can prophesy the future, and it is said he knows the hour and manner of his own death.

Against such a villain, Boothby sets a tale of pursuit and vendetta in the sensation style of the 1890s. Nikola's calm, occult power made him unlike the criminals of earlier fiction, and he returned in later Boothby novels. The book stands at the head of that series, where the supervillain first steps forward.
a-cumberland-vendetta:
John Fox Jr. opens in a cave above a Kentucky river, where a tall mountaineer and a boy with a squirrel rifle longer than himself step out into the rhododendrons. The cave was their childhood hiding place and stays their refuge when hunting. Below them lies a valley divided by an old feud between two families.

The tale follows the vendetta's code: ambush, reprisal, and young love growing across the line between the houses. Fox, who knew the Cumberland country well, writes the mountains, the cornfields on steep slopes, and the people's speech with a local's ear. His feud story became a small classic of Appalachian fiction, sadder than it is violent.
a-lecture-on-physical-development-and-it: Samuel Robert Calthrop lectures on physical development and its relations to mental and spiritual development. Delivered at Norwich, Connecticut, in August 1858, the lecture was printed in five thousand copies for free circulation. Calthrop addresses the American Institute of Instruction on body, mind, and spirit. The lecture links education with health and character. The plain talk links a sound body with a sound mind and heart.
a-monk-of-cruta:
A Monk of Cruta is an 1894 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, written early in his long career. Oppenheim later became one of the best-known English thriller writers of his time, but this book dates from before that fame. It survives as one of his earliest works of fiction, from the period when he was still finding his ground as a novelist.

Modern reprints present it as a fascinating novel of its period, and it is now scarce in early editions. For readers, its interest lies in seeing the young Oppenheim at work before the spy stories and international intrigues that made his name. The book preserves the starting point of a major popular career.
a-sketch-of-the-history-of-oneonta: Dudley Campbell sketches the history of Oneonta, New York, in this volume printed by the Herald and Democrat Press in 1883. The preface warns that the pages do not attempt a complete history, offering instead a sketch in five chapters. Advertisements for booksellers, flour merchants, and dry goods houses bound into the volume give the town's commercial face alongside its past.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-14-the-n:
A supplementary fourteenth volume closes the Beacon Lights of History, written not by John Lord but by recent writers after his death in 1894. The publishers explain the need: Lord could not summarise the last fifty years' achievement himself. His vivid, personal method ruled out a dry cyclopaedia of facts, so single essays take up single themes of the new era.

Invention and industry lead. One essay weighs John Ericsson, builder of the Monitor: a large measure of independence was necessary to his work, for a man who listened to everyone would never have accomplished it. In Ericsson the trait ran to an undue extreme, the writer concedes, and cost him collaborations. Steam, iron, and electricity get the biographical treatment Lord gave kings, in this posthumous survey of a transformed half-century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-grot:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Grottaferrata describes a Basilian monastery near Rome, on the Alban hills' lower slopes, sometimes said to stand on Cicero's Tusculanum. St. Nilus the Younger, a Calabrian Greek, founded it in 1004 after fleeing Saracen raids in 980 and wandering among monasteries without a permanent home.

Legend says Our Lady appeared at the site and bade Nilus found a church in her honour, and Gregory, Count of Tusculum, gave him the ground. Nilus died in December 1005, and his successors, above all the fourth abbot, St. Bartholomew, the second founder, built the abbey. Its monks' high repute drew many gifts, and its possessions grew numerous and widespread through a troubled history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-vo:
Alessandro Volta was an Italian physicist, born at Como in February 1745 and dead there in March 1827. His parents were not well off, so church relatives saw to his schooling. He finished his humanities at seventeen and showed his scientific bent at nineteen in letters to Abbé Nollet. His first paper of 1769 helped win him the chair of physics at the Como lyceum in 1774.

Volta worked with forethought throughout, never by mere chance, and his condensing electroscope and electrophorus of 1775 tested his contact theory of electricity. Seeking further proof, he built the voltaic pile, described in March 1800 to Sir Joseph Banks. It stacked discs of zinc and copper parted by wet cloth in a column, later improved as the crown of cups. Napoleon invited him to Paris in 1801, made him an associate of the Institute of France and later a senator of the Kingdom of Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andres-urdane:
Andres de Urdaneta, Augustinian, was born at Villafranca in 1498 and died in Mexico City in 1568. Orphaned, he studied Latin and philosophy, then became a captain in the Italian wars. Returning to Spain, he studied mathematics and astronomy, which drew him to seafaring, and in 1525 joined Jofre de Loaiza's Molucca expedition, serving eleven years.

On his return the Portuguese in Lisbon prosecuted him for telling his voyage. Charles V received him coldly. Wearied by adventure, he returned to Mexico and entered the Augustinian order. In 1564 the Audiencia equipped a Philippines expedition and offered Urdaneta command. He accompanied it but refused command; Miguel Lopez de Legazpi commanded. The expedition sailed on 21 November 1564. Legazpi stayed and sent Urdaneta back to find a return route. Leaving Cebu in July 1565, he sailed north for winds, took command, and reached Acapulco in October, when only he and Felipe de Salcedo could cast the anchors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aosta:
Aosta is an Italian diocese, a bishop's district under Turin, covering seventy-three towns in the province of Turin. St. Ursus is sometimes named as its first bishop, but that claim is greatly disputed; the first certainly known bishop is St. Eustasius, whose name with Aosta appears on a letter to Pope Leo I from the second Synod of Milan in 451. From the ninth century the list of prelates is fairly complete. Suppressed in 1802, the diocese was restored in 1817.

In the article's figures it counts 82,000 Catholics, eighty-seven parishes, 188 secular priests, twenty-four regulars, fifty-five seminarians, and 566 churches, chapels, or oratories. Its cathedral treasury holds a diptych, a two-panel carving, of the consul Anicius Probus from 406, found in 1833. St. Anselm of Canterbury was a native of Aosta, and St. Bernard de Menthon, its archdeacon, founded the Alpine hospice that bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apophthegmata:
Apophthegmata, sayings of the Fathers of the Desert, gathers the short sayings and stories of the hermits and monks who filled the Egyptian deserts in the fourth century. Collections in Latin, Greek, and Syriac preserve aphorisms and anecdotes that illustrate the spiritual life, ascetic and monastic principle, and Christian ethics. Rosweyde edited several Latin collections, Cotelier a Greek one, and Bedjan and Budge a Syriac collection, the last with an English translation.

Though arranged differently, the collections share most of their matter, and scholars agree the surviving literature is Greek in form, though much of it comes ultimately from Coptic sources. Sayings passed from master to disciple through the fourth century before they were written down, and the article traces how scattered talk hardened into books. Readers seeking desert wisdom will find here the sources behind countless later lives of saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augusta:
Augusta was a titular see of Cilicia in Asia Minor, a former bishopric kept on the books in name. Its bishops are listed for the years 363 to 434 in Gams. The entry is short, and most of its space goes to a warning: many Roman cities bore the same name, so readers must not confuse them. Several of those namesakes still flourish under modern names.

The list runs from Auch in southern France, ancient Augusta Auscorum, to London, ancient Augusta Trinobantum. Between them stand Leyden, Astorga, Aosta, Augst, Turin, Trier, and Augsburg, each with its own ancient Augusta name. The entry cites Lequien and Smith's dictionary of Greek and Roman geography for the identifications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-levi:
Benedict Levita, or Benedict the Deacon, names the supposed author of a forged set of ninth-century church laws, examined in this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. The collection, called capitularies, or royal church decrees, belongs to the Pseudo-Isidore group of forgeries. Its claim to come from the archives of Mainz, ordered by Archbishop Autgar, is shown to be false.

Internal clues place the forgery instead in the western Frankish lands, perhaps near Reims, after Autgar's death in 847. Its hostility to chorepiscopi, or rural assistant bishops, and its early use among the western Franks point that way. The entry is a piece of detective work on a fake that shaped medieval church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biretta:
The biretta, a square cap with three ridges worn by clergy from cardinals down, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Rubrics prescribe it at solemn Mass and other church functions. Its Italian name, more correctly beretta, likely comes from birrus, a rough hooded cloak, from a Greek word for flame colour.

A birettum appears by the tenth century, but like most costume history its story is tangled. Colours mark rank: scarlet for cardinals, purple for bishops, black for priests, with tassels and linings varying by custom. The entry is a short history of a hat that signals office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bogota:
Bogota, capital of Colombia, sits on a high plateau 8,700 feet above sea level, ringed by mountains except where the Funcha River cuts southwest. Spaniards settled it in 1538, and it became capital of New Granada in 1598 and of independent Colombia in 1819. Its isolation kept its old Spanish character, and its population stood at only 100,000.

The archdiocese, created by Pius IV in 1564, is Colombia's primatial see. It once held six suffragans, though Medellin was separated in 1902. Its remaining suffragans include Antioquia, Ibague, Nueva Pamplona, Socorro, and Tunja. Jesuits, Franciscans, Augustinians, and Salesians served the archdiocese, whose churches and schools the entry lists in detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calcutta:
The province of Calcutta covers much of old Bengal. Portuguese merchants trading from the mid-sixteenth century won leave from the Mogul emperor Akbar about 1571 to build at Hugli, raise churches, and baptize natives. By 1598 Hugli counted 5,000 Catholics, and Portuguese adventurers hired by native rulers settled riverbank bands called bandels, marrying native women and gathering converts known as topassees for their hats.

Bengal first answered to Cochin, then from 1606 to San Thomé de Meliapur, while Jesuits built a school and hospital at Hugli and churches at Chittagong. The province later grew into the archdiocese of Calcutta, with schools, charities, chaplains for railways and troops, and missions among the native peoples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caltanisetta:
Caltanisetta lies in a fertile Sicilian plain on the Salso River, beside the world's greatest sulphur mines, and its name is Arabic in origin. A great cavern at Caltabillotta is famed for the legend of a dragon driven out by the hermit Peregrinus, who chose the spot for penance. The city once belonged to Girgenti, but Gregory XVI made it a see in 1844, suffragan to Monreale, with Antonio Stromillo as first bishop.

Its notable churches are the cathedral Santa Maria Nuova and Santa Maria Vecchia, famed for a Saracen-Norman portal, a fine work of art. Caltanisetta counts 17 parishes, 182 churches and chapels, 225 secular priests, 145,000 Catholics, and houses for men and women religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caqueta:
Caquetá is an apostolic prefecture on Colombia's southern border, set in the angle between the Central Cordilleras and the Caquetá ranges along the river of the same name. A December 1902 accord between the government and the Holy See put almost all of Mocoa province in the new prefecture. Its erection decree dates from December 1904.

Capuchins of the Spanish province of Catalonia took charge of evangelizing the Indigenous peoples of the region. By 1906 two mission stations at Mocoa and Sibundoy held ten fathers and three lay brothers serving fourteen chapels. Some 12,000 converts lived among 40,000 others, with 245 baptisms, 130 marriages, and 118 funerals recorded that year, plus five schools teaching 178 children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-maratta:
Carlo Maratta was an Italian painter born at Camerino in the March of Ancona in May 1625 who died at Rome in December 1713. A child prodigy in design, he went to Rome to study under Andrea Sacchi, his lifelong friend and benefactor. Returning home and then coming back to Rome in 1650 with Cardinal Albrizio, governor of Ancona, he won Alexander VII's favor and many commissions.

Chief among them was Constantine destroying the idols for the Lateran Baptistery, a work that raised his standing at the Vatican. Clement XI knighted him in 1704 and gave him the Order of Christ, while Louis XIV made him painter in ordinary the same year after admiring his Daphne. Romans called him Maratti, he belonged to the Academy of St. Luke, and he proved highly skilled at cleaning and repairing frescoes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-porta:
Carlo Porta was a Milanese poet born in 1775 who died at Milan in January 1821. Schooled by Jesuits at Monza and in the Milan seminary, he found trade uncongenial and took Treasury posts at Venice and then Milan. He served the Cisalpine Republic. Still an Italian patriot, he welcomed the Austrians' return as a promise of peace and prosperity. At Milan, Foscolo and Monti were among his companions.

His fame rests on turning the Milanese dialect to poetic use with rare felicity, arguing the Romantic cause of Manzoni and Grossi in verse. He shines brightest in humorous pieces that sketch Milanese types, above all the misadventures of Giovannin Bongee. His dialect, the people's speech raised to masterly literary expression, anchors his standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caserta:
Caserta is a diocese in southern Italy, its city the provincial capital about twenty miles from Naples in a fertile and pleasant region. It rose under Lombards and Normans, its counts once powerful lords. It passed through noble families to the Gaetani, who gave it to Charles III, King of Naples. He remade it as a second Versailles, with Vanvitelli's magnificent royal castle and fine aristocratic residences nearby.

No one knows when Caserta became a see, but Ranulfo, elected in 1113 and confirmed by the Archbishop of Capua, is its first known bishop. Later bishops include Andrea, who finished the cathedral belfry in 1234, and Azzone and Secondo, champions of church liberty. Mirandola studied Aristotle, Mandina promoted an anti-Turk league, and Caballo won fame for piety and preaching. Pius VII joined the see to Caiazzo in 1818, Pius IX split them again, and the diocese now counts 96,800 people in 51 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-castellaneta:
Castellaneta is a diocese suffragan to Taranto, its city in Lecce province in southern Italy, some twenty-four miles from Taranto. Nothing is known of the city before 1080. That year Robert, Duke of Tarentum, took it and expelled its Byzantine inhabitants, probably creating the see, the same year Tarentum became a metropolitan see. Joannes is the first Bishop of Castellaneta mentioned by name.

A record also names a Bishop of Mottola, otherwise unknown, who died in 1040, succeeded by a certain Liberius. The diocese counts 38,000 people in six parishes, with 41 churches and chapels, 69 priests, two houses for men and six for women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charismata:
Charismata is the Greek word for gifts flowing from God's love, from redemption to shared comfort. In a narrower sense it means the spiritual graces given to every Christian for his task in the Church. In its narrowest sense it names extraordinary graces given to individuals for others' good.
