St. Paul lists these in First Corinthians: wisdom and knowledge in speech, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, tongues, and their interpretation, with apostles, prophets, doctors, helps, and governments added. They were foretold by Joel and promised by Christ to believers.

The gifts divide into those serving the Church's inner life and those serving its outward growth. Inner gifts build up believers themselves. Outer ones carry the faith beyond the community. Both kinds are given not for private display but for the benefit of others. A gift is measured by the service it renders to the whole body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concordia-ven:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers Concordia Veneta, also called Julia, suffragan of Venice. Romans named it Colonia Concordia, between the Tagliamento and Livenza rivers near the Adriatic. Today only ruins and the ancient cathedral remain. Attila destroyed it in the fifth century, and Lombards again in 606, after which it never rose. Its eighty-nine martyrs, slain under Diocletian, draw great veneration. Clarissimus, its first known bishop, helped prolong the Schism of the Three Chapters at Aquileia's synod in 579.

Augustinus, later bishop, signed the schismatics' petition to Emperor Mauricius in 590. Bishop Johannes moved the residence to Caorle in 606, keeping the Concordia title. Medieval bishops lived near the old cathedral and wielded temporal power they could not hold. In 1587, under Matteo Sanudo, the residence moved finally to Portogruaro. The diocese counted 258,315 people, with 129 parishes, 231 churches and chapels, 264 secular and 2 regular priests, nine women's houses, and a Pius X college for African missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantine-c:
Georges Goyau's entry covers the Diocese of Constantine, called Constantiniana, in Algeria's Constantine district. Separated from Algiers in 1866, its bishop took the title Bishop of Constantine and Hippo in 1867. Cirta, renamed for Constantine, held a bishop's see from the second century until the Muslim invasion.

Valerian's persecution martyred Agapius, Secundinus, soldier Aemilianus, and virgins Tertulla and Antonia there. Fifth-century territory held 195 dioceses, including Hippo, governed by Saint Augustine. In 1842 Mgr Dupuch brought Augustine's right arm from Pavia to Hippo, its feast kept yearly. Lavigerie bought Hippo's hill in 1880, its new basilica blessed on 11 March 1900. Before the 1901 law Lazarists, Little Brothers of Mary, and White Fathers worked there; now only the last remain. At 1905's close, population reached 137,041, with five pastorates, sixty-seven mission parishes, and seventeen state-paid curacies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damietta:
A historical entry describes Damietta, an Egyptian titular see at the mouth of the Nile's Phatnitic branch, whose prosperity rose as its metropolis Pelusium declined. Four bishops are known, from 431 to 879. Arabs took it under Caliph Omar and held it against Greeks and against Amaury I of Jerusalem.

Jean de Brienne captured it in 1219 after a fifteen-month siege, of whose 70,000 people only 3,000 survived. Saint Francis visited the crusader camp and preached to Sultan Malek Kemel. Franks lost it in 1221, Saint Louis retook it in June 1249 and turned the mosque El-Fatah into a church, then surrendered it as ransom in 1250. The sultan destroyed it in 1251, and fishermen's shelters among the ruins grew into the modern town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-famagusta:
Famagusta is a titular see on the east coast of Cyprus. Its name comes from Ammochostos, not from Fama Augusti as once claimed. Guy de Lusignan was crowned king there in 1191. Its great church of St Nicholas later became a mosque under Turkish rule.

A Latin diocese flourished there from the twelfth century to the sixteenth century. Genoese took the city in 1374, and Venetians held it until 1571. After a ten-month Turkish siege, the commander Bragadino was burned alive. The city then shrank to a poor village of about a thousand souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-francisc:
A seventeenth-century Spanish Franciscan, Francisco de Ayeta spent his career defending his order's missions in Mexico and New Mexico. He served in turn as visitor of the Holy Gospel province, as its agent at Madrid, and as the Inquisition's commissary for New Spain. The entry presents him as a forceful writer who fought the move to strip the regular orders of their parishes.

Ayeta visited far-flung missions in person and warned Madrid as early as 1678 that New Mexico stood exposed before a Pueblo rising. His warning won troops for Santa Fe, but too late: the Pueblos rose in August 1680, and New Mexico stayed out of Spanish hands for fourteen years. When two thousand hungry refugees reached El Paso, he was the first to feed and clothe them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-juan-bau:
Juan Bautista, born in Mexico City in 1555, became a Franciscan teacher at the convent of St. Francis, lecturing in theology and metaphysics. He held office as definitor of his province and as guardian of Tezcuco, Tlatelolco, and Tacuba in turn. The entry follows a man who at first cared little for the tongue of the people around him, then mastered it.

Though born among Nahuatl speakers, Bautista long looked past their language, but contact with his order's schools changed his mind, and he soon knew Nahuatl well. Ten of his works in that language were written before 1607, and several were printed at Mexico, though others survive by title alone. His death date is unknown, placed roughly between 1606 and 1615.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-barle:
Gabriel Barletta, a Dominican preacher of the late fifteenth century, was held up in his lifetime as the model orator. Born, by one account, at Barletta in Naples, or by another at Aquino, he likely studied under Saint Antoninus. He died sometime after 1480. Italy kept a proverb for him: he who cannot preach like Barletta cannot preach at all.

His sermons, printed at Brixen in 1497, ran to thirteen editions in eighty years, with Venice 1577 the best. In form they are plain homilies on virtues and vices, sparing no weakness of the age, with biting sarcasm and at times coarse mimicry. Some scholars doubt he wrote them all, yet most accept them as his, since they breathe his times and match his fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-sioni:
Gabriel Sionita, a learned Maronite born on Mount Lebanon in 1577, gave his scholarship to the great Paris polyglot Bible. Brought to Rome at seven, he kept Arabic as his mother tongue while learning Latin, Syriac, and some Hebrew. He took priesthood late, at Paris, at forty-five. With John Hesronita he was brought to Paris to serve the polyglot project.

Sionita held the Sorbonne chair of Semitic tongues and revised nearly all its Syriac and Arabic texts, turning them into Latin. But funds promised by the French clergy never reached him, quarrels and money troubles followed, and Cardinal Richelieu had him jailed at Vincennes in 1640. Freed after three months on pledges, he finished his vast task before his death at seventy-one in 1648.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaeta:
Gaeta, an archdiocese on the Campanian coast of southern Italy, began as the ancient town of Caieta on a headland above the sea. Strabo calls it an Ionian colony of Samos, while legend names it for Caieta, nurse of Aeneas. Its port served trade and war alike, and its mild climate drew praise from the ancients. The tomb of Plancus still stands among its relics.

As Byzantine power faded, Gaeta grew into a small republic under a duke and held the line against Saracen raids, aiding Leo IV at Ostia in 847. Normans, French, Spanish, and Austrians fought over its strategic rock in turn. In February 1861 it fell as Francis II of Naples' final refuge, sealing Italy's union. Popes from Gelasius II to Pius IX had also sheltered there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-della:
Giacomo Della Porta was an architect and sculptor born on Lake Lugano in 1541, who died in 1604. A pupil of Michelangelo, he succeeded Vignola as architect of St. Peter's. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his churches, palaces, and fountains across Rome and Genoa, and his role in shaping the Baroque manner.

With Domenico Fontana he finished the dome and lantern of St. Peter's by 1590 or 1592. He completed Vignola's plan for Il Gesu, whose two-story facade became a model for Baroque churches far and wide. At Genoa he built the Annunziata as a columned basilica, and in Rome he added fountains at the Capitol and the Piazza Mattei. He kept something of Michelangelo's spirit without falling into the excesses of the later Baroque.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gines-perez-d:
Ginés Pérez de Hita was a Spanish writer born at Murcia, of whom little is known beyond his life in the second half of the sixteenth century. He probably fought in campaigns against the Moors from 1560 onward, learning their customs and seeing the remains of their splendor. A Catholic Encyclopedia article makes his fame rest on one double work, the Guerras civiles de Granada.

Its first part, printed at Zaragoza in 1595, claims to translate an Arabic book by a Moor of Granada on the Zegries and Abencerrages. The claim is false, and the book is really a novel founded on fact. Its second part, on the later Moorish uprising, appeared at Barcelona in 1619 and reads as history with the character of a novel. His language stays strikingly modern, pure, terse, and sonorous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-giud:
Giovanni Giuda Giona Battista, born Jehuda Jona Ben-Isaac, was a Hebrew scholar born of Jewish parents at Safed in Galilee in 1588, who died at Rome in 1668. As a Jewish rabbi he traveled widely through Europe, and during a stay in Poland he became a Catholic. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a convert who turned his learning to the Church's service.

After his conversion the King of Poland sent him to Constantinople, where he was arrested as a spy and barely escaped through the Venetian ambassador. Later in Italy he taught Hebrew and Aramaic at Pisa and at the Propaganda in Rome. His pupil Giulio Bartolocci owed him the plan of the great Bibliotheca Magna Rabbinica. His chief work rendered the Gospels from Latin into Hebrew, published at Rome in 1668.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-casa:
Girolamo Casanata was a cardinal born at Naples in 1620, who died at Rome in 1700. Son of a member of the kingdom's supreme council, he studied law, practiced in the courts, then entered the service of the Church. Under Innocent X he rose fast, governing Sabina, Fabriano, Ancona, and Camerino in turn. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a curial career of uncommon wisdom and wide experience.

Alexander VII sent him as inquisitor to Malta in 1658, and later popes made him consultor of congregations, assessor of the Holy Office, and secretary of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. Named cardinal-deacon in 1673 and cardinal-priest in 1686, he became Librarian of the Vatican in 1693. His Casanatense Library still keeps 1125 manuscript volumes of opinions, reports, and statements on matters before the Holy See.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-house-of-mala:
The Malatesta were an Italian family prominent in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, famous in Dante's poetry and in early Renaissance annals. Their founder, Malatesta da Verrucchio, led the Guelphs in Romagna and seized Rimini in 1295 by slaughtering chief members of the rival Ghibelline Parcitati. Thenceforth the family ruled cities across Romagna and the March of Ancona.

They held Rimini until 1500, Pesaro until 1446, plus Fano, Cesena, Fossombrone, and Cervia, sometimes by papal investiture and sometimes by the sword. Many Malatesti were notorious for crime and cruelty, but two stood out for virtue. Carlo backed the church at Constance, and Galeotto Roberto became a Franciscan and shortened his life by austerities. Giovanni, called Gianciotto, is famed for the domestic tragedy of 1285 in Dante's Inferno.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idiota:
Idiota, or Raymundus Jordanus, was the pen name of a learned, pious writer of old whose identity stayed unknown for centuries. The name need not carry its modern sense: idiota in Greek means private, simple, or peculiar, and the writer likely used it to signal that he was a person of no consequence. His works soon became widely known, though he himself remained unknown.

The Bibliotheca Patrum printed them several times, and his Contemplations on Divine Love often appear in small manuals beside meditations of Augustine, Bernard, and Anselm. A 1618 collection placed him among tenth-century writers, and Bellarmine put his flowering about 902. Father Theophilus Raynaud first discovered that Raymundus Jordanus wrote the works, explaining the find in his 1641 preface to the Oculus Mysticus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeronimo-mend:
Jerónimo Mendieta, a Spanish Franciscan missionary born at Vitoria in 1525 and dead in Mexico City in 1604. He took the habit at Bilbao young and reached New Spain in late June 1554. Eager to convert Indigenous peoples, he mastered the Mexican tongue with zeal.

A speech defect weakened Mendieta's Castilian, so he did not preach to Spaniards, yet in Indigenous language he spoke clearly from the pulpit without stammering. At Tlaxcala he likely served under Motolinía, last survivor of the first twelve Franciscans. His province so trusted him that a chapter let him pick all provincial officers himself, to everyone's content.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joaquin-acost:
Joaquín Acosta, a Colombian soldier-scholar, surveyed his country between Socorro and the Magdalena in 1834, then explored western Colombia from Antioquia to Anserma. That was seven years later, studying landforms, natural history, and traces of native peoples. In 1845 he travelled to Spain, examining colonial papers on Colombia.

Three years later Acosta published his Compendium on New Granada's discovery and colonisation, with a map fair for its time and rich notes on books and lives. His account of conqueror Quesada's writings is incomplete and often wrong. Yet his lives of churchmen who preserved Colombia's early knowledge, from Zamora and Fresle to Lugo's language work, remain a guide for students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-de-acost:
Jose de Acosta was a Spanish Jesuit whose Natural and Moral History of the Indies became a classic of the New World. Born at Medina del Campo in 1540 to well-to-do parents, he entered the Jesuits at thirteen, four brothers following him. He lectured in theology at Ocana, and was sent to Lima in 1569, a year after the Jesuits reached Peru.

At Lima and Cuzco he taught theology and visited Jesuit colleges. He was elected provincial in 1576, founding colleges at Arequipa, Potosi, Chuquisaca, Panama, and La Paz despite the viceroy Toledo's opposition. His wide travels gave him practical knowledge of the vast province and its native peoples. At Lima's provincial council of 1582 he played a leading part. After Mexico and Rome, where he taught at the Roman College in 1594, he died as rector of Salamanca in 1600, praised by eighteenth-century naturalists for his knowledge of South American flora.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-anchie:
Joseph Anchieta was a Jesuit missionary called the Apostle of Brazil. Born on Tenerife in 1553, he studied at Coimbra, joined the Society of Jesus at seventeen, and sailed to Brazil hoping the climate would mend his damaged health. He stayed about forty-four years, teaching Latin in what was likely America's first classical school and learning the native tongue.

Anchieta wrote songs, plays, and religious books for converts and once stayed willingly as a hostage among the Tamuin people. Captivity is also credited with a poem of almost five thousand verses, composed from memory. Later rector and provincial of Brazil, he was declared Venerable by the Church, and his beatification was under consideration when this entry appeared.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-arricivi:
Juan Arricivita was an eighteenth-century Mexican Franciscan missionary and historian. Little is known of his life beyond his posts as prefect and commissary at Querétaro's College of Propaganda Fide in New Spain. He was a zealous and able missionary, highly esteemed throughout his order.

Arricivita earns special mention for the Chronicles of Querétaro's second volume, published at Mexico in 1792. The book is invaluable for the history of missions and colonization in northwestern Mexico, Arizona, and California. It continues the earlier first part by Isidro Félix Espinosa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knights-of-ma:
The Knights of Malta form the greatest of the military orders in reach and in lifespan, still alive at the time of writing. They were Hospitallers of Jerusalem until 1309, Knights of Rhodes from 1309 to 1522, and Knights of Malta from 1530.

Their certain founder is Gerald, or Gerard, named in Pope Paschal II's bull of 1113 as head of the Jerusalem hospital. Older pilgrim hostels existed, Frankish under Charlemagne, Hungarian under St. Stephen, and Italian from Amalfi merchants about 1050. But Gerard's house was its own master from the start, followed St. John the Baptist rather than St. John of Alexandria, and kept St. Augustine's Rule rather than St. Benedict's. Crusader gratitude then won it lands and income across Jerusalem, Sicily, Italy, and Provence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litta:
Litta was a noble Milanese family that gave the Church two cardinals, Alfonso and Lorenzo, two centuries apart. Alfonso, born in 1608, governed the Marches for Innocent X and became Archbishop of Milan in 1652. He died at Rome in 1679, known as learned, generous, and bold in guarding church rights against Spain's officers.

Lorenzo, born in 1756, shone as a scholar and as a diplomat. As nuncio to Poland he pleaded with Kosciuszko for churchmen and saved one condemned bishop. He pressed the partitioning powers to guard church property, a pledge Catherine II broke. Sent to Moscow and St. Petersburg, he won back six Latin dioceses and three Ruthenian ones before his death in 1820.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-costa:
Lorenzo Costa was a Ferrarese painter, born in 1460 and dead at Mantua in 1535. Likely a pupil of Tura or Cossa, he settled at Bologna at twenty-three under the Bentivogli, sharing a shop with Francia, who worked as a goldsmith.

Friendship shaped both men: Costa's wider imagination and surer drawing may have pulled Francia from goldsmith work into painting. His first Bologna fresco dates to 1480, his greatest altarpiece to 1497, and the pair painted jointly for the Misericordia. Driven out with the Bentivogli in 1509, Costa served the Gonzaga at Mantua, where his late frescoes still show bold colour, rich architecture, and easy drapery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-di-pi:
Lorenzo di Pietro, called Vecchietta, was a Sienese painter, sculptor, goldsmith, and architect, born in 1412 and dead in 1480. Pupil of Taddeo Bartoli and Giacomo della Quercia, he followed Donatello in sculpture and Sienese custom in painting.

His finest work fills the Hospital of Santa Maria della Scala at Siena. There he gave a chapel to Our Lady, with frescoes of the Annunciation, Nativity, and Last Judgment, plus a bronze Risen Christ in Donatello's harsher mode. Baptistery frescoes, a Madonna in the gallery, and an Assumption at Pienza round out a career that also taught Francesco di Giorgio and Neroccio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magna-carta:
Magna Carta was the charter of liberties forced from King John of England in 1215. Henry III confirmed it, with changes, in 1216, 1217, and 1225. English-speaking peoples have long prized it. They treat it as the first great document of England's distinct constitutional story.

Its roots lie in feudal abuse under Stephen. Henry II then built stronger royal rule. John's loss of French lands and his constant demands for money pushed barons into open resistance. Its chapters follow no neat plan. Only a couple read as broad statements of principle. Critics call it backward-looking and baronial in interest. Yet its exact clauses faded with time, while its symbolic weight grew far beyond what its makers meant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malta:
Malta covers the Maltese islands, chiefly Malta, Gozo, and Comino, lying 58 miles south of Sicily. Malta served as headquarters of the British Mediterranean fleet and the sea's chief coaling station. That key position brought wealth enough to support a people far larger than the islands' size suggests. Civil population reached about 205,059 in 1906, with over 99 percent Catholic.

Government rested on an Executive Council of eleven besides the governor, and a Legislative Council beside it. Phoenicians colonised the islands very early. Arab rule left its chief mark in the Maltese tongue, Semitic and close to Arabic. Malta passed with Sicily to the Swabian emperors in 1199, then to Charles of Anjou after Beneventum in 1266. The Order of St John waned with Ottoman decline. Church history runs beside civil history here, from a Church founded by St Paul in tradition to clergy who long led the people as their natural guides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mantelletta:
Mantelletta was an outer vestment reaching to the knees, open in front, with slits instead of sleeves at the sides. Cardinals, bishops, and prelates di mantelletta wore it. For cardinals its colour was ordinarily red. In penitential seasons and mourning it turned violet, and on Gaudete and Laetare Sundays it turned rose.

For other dignitaries the same distinctions held, but the colour was violet, or black with a violet border. Members of orders kept their habit's colour, as did entitled abbots. Only cardinals and court bishops or prelates wore it in silk. Its likely kin are the mantellum of cardinals in Gregory X's Ordo and of prelates in Petrus Amelius's Ordo, a scapular-like vestment. The longer mantellone, with wing-like sleeves, differed from it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcus-eremit:
Marcus Eremita, Mark the Hermit, was a fifth-century theologian and ascetic writer of note. Kunze's study, now widely followed, places him as superior of a laura at Ancyra, then as an old man a hermit in the desert east of Palestine near St Sabas. He lived at Nestorius's time and likely died before Chalcedon in 451.

Older guesses put him elsewhere. Nicephorus Callistus made him a pupil of John Chrysostom. Bellarmine took him for the monk who foretold ten more years for Emperor Leo VI in 900, a view Tillemont refuted. Byzantine calendars matched him with an Egyptian monk of Palladius, from the fourth century. Kerameus's find of his work against Nestorius settled his period. His writings cover the spiritual law, justification by works, penance, baptism, anger and lust, fasting, humility, and Melchisedek, with a treatise against Nestorians added. Practical rather than mystical, he follows the Antiochene school and Chrysostom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-aspilc:
Martin Aspilcueta, called Navarrus or Doctor Navarrus, was a famed Spanish canonist and moral theologian, born in Navarre in 1491 and dead at Rome in 1586. He then held the same chair fourteen years at Salamanca and seven at Coimbra in Portugal.

At eighty he travelled to Rome to defend his friend Archbishop Bartolomeo Carranza of Toledo before the Inquisition. He failed to clear Carranza, yet popes honoured him as a fount of learning and prudence. His humility, disinterest, and charity were proverbial, and he lived to ninety-five, buried at Rome's San Antonio de' Portoghesi. His Manuale sive Enchiridion Confessariorum et Poenitentium of 1568, first Spanish, long served as a classic school and practice text. On benefice revenues he held that beneficed clergy might spend fruits only on their own needs and the poor. His complete works filled three folio volumes at Rome in 1590.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matteo-of-aqu:
Matteo of Aquasparta was a celebrated Italian Franciscan, born at Aquasparta in Todi diocese, Umbria, about 1235 and dead at Rome on 29 October 1302. Matteo joined the order at Todi, took a Master of Theology degree at Paris, and taught for a time at Bologna.

When John Peckham became Canterbury archbishop in 1279, Matteo succeeded him in 1280 as Lector sacri Palatii apostolici, reader of theology to the papal Curia. In 1287 Montpellier's chapter elected him Franciscan general, succeeding Arlotto of Prato. When former general Girolamo Masci became Pope Nicholas IV in February 1288, he made Matteo cardinal of San Lorenzo in Damaso. With the older Franciscan school he preferred Augustinianism to the pronounced Aristotelianism of St Thomas Aquinas. His chief work, the acute Quaestiones disputatae on various subjects, saw one volume at Quaracchi in 1903, with editing since discontinued.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minnesota:
Minnesota, one of the North Central States of the American Union, lies midway between the continent's eastern and western shores and midway between the Gulf of Mexico and Hudson Bay. It stretches about 400 miles north to south and 354 miles at its greatest breadth, covering 84,287 square miles, of which 5,637 are water, thanks to some 10,000 inland lakes. It is bounded by Canada, Lake Superior, Wisconsin, Iowa, and the Dakotas.

Its name comes from the Minnesota River, from mini, water, and sotah, sky-coloured. When white explorers arrived, two great divisions of the American race inhabited the region. Bishop Mathias of Dubuque, whose diocese covered all Minnesota, visited Fort Snelling in 1839 and sent Father Lucien Galtier as missionary in 1840. Galtier settled on the present site of St. Paul and built a log chapel named for the Apostle of the Gentiles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moneta:
Moneta of Cremona, who died at Bologna in 1240, was a theologian and one of the earliest followers of Saint Dominic. Before joining the order in 1220 he taught philosophy at the University of Bologna. His learning, depth of thought and lucid teaching won him a wide name.

He first shunned the Dominicans, fearing a popular preacher would dim his own standing. One sermon he attended at his pupils' urging moved him so deeply that he entered the order himself. He grew known as much for holiness as for eloquent, learned disputes with heretics. His intense study cost him his sight late in life. His Summa against the Cathars and Waldensians was widely read in its day and first printed in 1743.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monita-secret:
The Monita Secreta purports to be a secret code of instructions from Acquaviva, fifth general of the Jesuits. It tells superiors how to grow the order's wealth and power. Young men of promise are to be lured in with their estates. Wealthy widows are to be coaxed away from remarrying. Jesuits are to be pushed toward bishoprics, rival orders discredited, and leavers blackened.

This entry shows the document to be a forgery. Its author was Jerome Zahorowski, a Pole dismissed from the Society in 1611. It first circulated in manuscript at Cracow in 1612 and was printed there in 1614. Shifting tales surrounded where it was found. The entry follows its later career as anti-Jesuit propaganda, its many editions and translations, and the evidence that unmasks its true author.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mozzetta:
The mozzetta is a short cape-shaped garment covering the shoulders and reaching only to the elbow. It is open in front and fastened by small buttons, with a tiny purely ornamental hood at the neck. The right to wear it belongs properly only to the pope, cardinals, exempt abbots, abbots general and the four prelates di fiochetti. Others need a special privilege.

Cardinals wear it over the mantelletta, bishops without it and only inside their own jurisdiction. Privileged canons may use it only in church or when the chapter appears as a body. The pope's is always red except for a white one in Easter week, edged with ermine in winter. A cardinal's turns pink on Gaudete and Laetare Sundays and violet in penitential seasons and mourning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-stig:
Mystical stigmata are the marks of Christ's Passion borne on hands, feet, side or brow by many ecstatics, with matching and intense sufferings. Those are visible stigmata. Others feel only the sufferings, without outward marks, and those are called invisible stigmata. History attests the facts so firmly that unbelievers no longer dispute them as a rule. They seek only to explain them naturally.

Saint Catherine of Siena at first bore visible marks, but through humility she asked that they be made invisible, and her prayer was heard. The same happened with Saint Catherine de Ricci, a Florentine Dominican of the sixteenth century, and several others. Suffering is the essential part of visible stigmata. Its substance is pity for Christ, sharing in his sorrows, and expiation for sins committed unceasingly in the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-north-dakota:
North Dakota, carved from the Louisiana Purchase, grew slowly through Indian wars, trapping, and railroads into statehood in 1889. Lewis and Clark wintered near Bismarck in 1804, Astor's men met Sioux on the Missouri in 1811, and the territory took shape in 1861 under Governor William Jayne.

Rolling prairie rises from the Red River valley toward the west, watered by the Missouri, Red, Sheyenne, and James rivers. The entry records its counties, wheat lands, and Catholic missions, with priests, parishes, and schools serving settlers across a thinly peopled state. Its main rivers are the Missouri, Red, Sheyenne, James, and Mouse, with their tributaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-paruta:
Paolo Paruta was a Venetian historian and statesman, born at Venice on 14 May 1540 and dead there on 6 December 1598. Of Luccan stock, he gave his youth to letters, philosophy, and poetry, above all history and political science. He stood at the century's end where Machiavelli had stood at its start, though in a different way, among newly ennobled men who debated politics at the Morosini house.

That liberal party took power in 1582, after Paruta had served as historiographer, funeral orator for Lepanto's dead in 1572, and envoy's companion to Maximilian II. He then became Savio di Terraferma, senator, commissioner of Cadore, governor of Brescia, ambassador to Rome, procurator of Saint Mark, and provveditore of fortresses. His Cyprus War and Venetian History, written for the state, are praised for truth and fairness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-regesta:
Papal regesta are the copies, usually entered in special registry volumes, of papal letters and official papers kept in the papal archives. The name also covers modern printed editions that list such papers in date order with careful summaries of their substance. Their beginnings likely predate Constantine, though no direct proof survives for the earliest period.

Growth of papal correspondence shows by the late second century, in the Easter controversy, and by the mid-third century, in the Decian persecution and the baptism dispute. Roman officials needed old letters at hand for like cases, so copies were surely made before dispatch and kept at the central administration. The entry traces the registers from early fragments through medieval volumes to modern scholarly editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-of-samos:
Paul of Samosata was Bishop of Antioch, deposed after several synods about 264 to 266. Dionysius of Alexandria wished to attend the first but infirmity barred him, while Firmilian of Caesarea, Gregory Thaumaturgus, his brother Athenodorus, and many others came. Paul held the civil post of procurator ducenarius and enjoyed Zenobia of Palmyra's protection. Wealthy, with many flattering bishops behind him, he declared himself orthodox, and early meetings left bishops satisfied.

At a later synod he was condemned but promised to retract, and failed to do so. A final council met, Firmilian dying en route, and Malchion, Antioch's learned priest and head of its Greek letters school, plainly convicted Paul of heresy in debate and won his deposition. Malchion's synodal letter, kept in part by Eusebius, charges Paul with illicit wealth, pride, worldliness, a lofty pulpit, and insulting those who would not flatter him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pforta:
Pforta was a Cistercian monastery near Naumburg on the Saale, standing from 1137 to 1540. Its story starts at Schmölln, where Count Bruno founded a Benedictine house in 1127 with 1,100 hides of land. The venture failed, and Bishop Udo I replaced the Benedictines with Cistercians from Walkenried in 1132, then moved the house to Pforta in 1137 with arable land, forest, and two farms.

Pforta, named for the narrow valley that gates Thuringia, honoured Our Lady under its first abbot, Adalbert. Under the third abbot it founded daughter houses in Meissen and Silesia, sent monks to Livonia in 1205, and grew tenfold in possessions within 140 years. Strife at the turn of the fourteenth century only renewed its vigour. The monks left no chronicles, so little is known of its inner spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-augusta:
Port Augusta diocese, suffragan of Adelaide in South Australia, was created in 1887. It stretches from latitude twenty-five south to the Murray River, between Queensland and New South Wales east and West Australia west. At its start it carried heavy debt, and its eleven thousand Catholics shrank under periodic droughts. Port Augusta town crowns Spencer's Gulf, and its fine stone cathedral overlooks the water.

John O'Reily, consecrated at Sydney on 1 May 1888, was the first bishop. His chief work was clearing diocesan debts, especially the cathedral's. He brought the Sisters of the Good Samaritan to Port Pirie in 1890 and moved to Adelaide as archbishop in January 1895. James Maher, consecrated in April 1896 after serving as vicar-general and administrator, faced nine straight years of drought across most of the diocese. The entry looks to future railways linking West Australia and Port Darwin to grow the small Catholic population.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raccolta:
Raccolta, Italian for a collection, is a book of prayers and pious exercises to which popes have attached indulgences. This encyclopedia entry gives the full title of the last official edition, printed at Rome in 1898. It is a collection of prayers and good works for which the Supreme Pontiffs have granted the holy indulgences. Telesforo Galli, a consultor of the Congregation of Indulgences, first published the Raccolta at Rome in 1807.

A decree of 30 November 1825, printed in the sixth edition, recognizes the indulgences as authentic. A decree of 13 November 1843, in the eleventh edition, the last Galli published, praises the work as most useful for all the faithful, living and dead. Later editions came from Aloysius Prinzivalli, substitute secretary of the congregation, under a decree of 15 December in the 1850s. No full translation may appear without the congregation's approval, though an approved English edition exists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabrata:
Sabrata is a titular see in Tripolitana, a Phoenician town on Africa's northern coast between the two Syrtes. With Oea and Leptis Magna it gave the Greek name Tripolis to the region. Its Phoenician name, found on coins and an inscription at Thevesta, was hellenized Abrotomon, though Pliny treats them as two distinct towns. Under Rome, Sabrata gained colonial rank; Vespasian's first wife Flavia Domitilla was the daughter of Statilius Capella of Sabrata. Justinian later fortified the town and built a beautiful church there.

In the Middle Ages it remained an important market, where interior natives brought their corn. Sabrata is now Zouagha, a small town Europeans call Tripoli Vecchia, fifty miles west of Tripoli. Its ruins, just north of the village, are crumbled ramparts, an amphitheatre, and a landing-stage. Four bishops are known: Pompey, Nados, Vincent, and Leo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacra-romana-:
The Sacra Romana Rota, re-established by Pius X in Sapienti Consilio of 29 June 1908, is one of three tribunals of that constitution. It takes all contentious cases that must come before the Holy See and require judicial investigation with proof, except major cases. It hears first-instance cases, including criminal ones, which the pope reserves for his own judgment or refers to the Rota for decision.

It decides them even in second and third instance. It is also the appeal court for cases already tried in episcopal tribunals of first instance. It decides in last instance cases tried by any inferior tribunal of second or further instance. The Rota is composed of auditors, ranking as prelates, appointed by the pope, who must be priests with doctorates in theology and canon law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salta:
Salta, an Argentine diocese covering the civil provinces of Salta and Jujuy in the far north, was created on 17 February 1807 from the old diocese of Córdoba del Tucumán. Until 1898 it also held Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, and Catamarca, since detached as new dioceses. Its short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists bishops and religious houses.

Nicolás Videla del Pino served as first bishop, followed by Buenaventura Rizo Patrón, Pablo Padilla y Bárcena, and the then bishop Matías Linares y Sanzetenea. The diocese owns a handsome cathedral and seminary and runs a printing plant issuing the Catholic daily Tribuna Popular. Redemptorists give missions, Salesians run schools, and sisters of the Good Shepherd and other orders serve the northern provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samosata:
Samosata, a titular see in Augusta Euphratensis suffragan of Hierapolis, was capital of Commagene, whose kings were kin to the Seleucids. Mithridates I Callinicus died in 96 before Christ, his son Antiochus I died before 31, and after tangled successions Tiberius joined Commagene to Syria in 17. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia unwinds a small kingdom's dynastic maze.

Caligula gave the land to Antiochus IV Epiphanes in 38, Claudius restored him in 41, and Caesonius Paetus deposed him for good in 72, sending his sons to Rome. A civil metropolis under Hadrian, Samosata housed the Sixteenth Legion Flavia Firma and ended several military roads. Birthplace of Lucian the satirist and of Paul, bishop of Antioch, it later kept its place as a Christian see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarepta:
Sarepta, a titular see in Phoenicia Prima suffragan of Tyre, first appears in an Egyptian traveller's account from the fourteenth century before Christ. Obadiah calls it Canaan's northern boundary. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gathers Bible, Josephus, Pliny, and pilgrim guides around a small coastal town.

Sennacherib captured it in 701 before Christ. In Ahab's time it answered to Sidon, and there Elijah multiplied a poor widow's meal and oil and raised her son from death, an act of charity Christ recalled in Luke's Gospel. Near the place, Christ may have healed the Canaanite woman's daughter, praised for her faith. By the sixth century pilgrims called Sarepta a small town, but very Christian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saskatchewan-:
Saskatchewan and Alberta, twin provinces of the Canadian west, were born the same day, 1 September 1905, by one Dominion act giving them identical constitutions. Saskatchewan takes its name from the Kissiskatchiwan, or Swift Current river, whose branches drain it eastward. Alberta honours St Albert borough near Edmonton, named for Father Albert Lacombe, veteran missionary of the far west. Their joint entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia surveys a new west.

Saskatchewan formed from Assiniboia, Saskatchewan, and eastern Athabasca districts, while Alberta came from the old Alberta territory and western Athabasca. Both run from 49 to 60 degrees north, with Saskatchewan between 102 and 110 degrees west and Alberta's western edge along the Rockies' crest. The entry covers land, peoples, and the Church's missions, schools, and dioceses across the prairie provinces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-serafino-porr:
Serafino Porrecta, born Capponi at Porrecta in 1536, was a Dominican theologian who died at Bologna in 1614. He entered the order at Bologna in 1552 and devoted his life wholly to study, teaching, writing, and preaching. His fame rests on commenting on Saint Thomas's Summa, and he also wrote valued commentaries on books of both Testaments. As a professor he taught philosophy, dogmatic and moral theology, and Sacred Scripture.

In 1606 he was invited to teach theology and Scripture to Carthusians near Bologna, but two years later he was recalled to the city, where he died. Bologna's people honored him as a saint, miracles were attested through his intercession, and his body was moved in 1615 to the Dominican church. His commentaries, joined with Cajetan's, long ranked among the most prized aids to students of the Summa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-south-dakota:
South Dakota, admitted to the Union on 2 November 1889 as the thirty-ninth state, is described here through its boundaries, landscape, people, and church life. The entry opens with the state's formal borders, drawn from Minnesota and Iowa westward to the 27th meridian and south to Nebraska. And gives its area as 76,850 square miles of generally rolling country.

Later sections follow settlement, population, and the Catholic Church's growth across the prairies, with dioceses, parishes, and institutions taking shape alongside farms and towns. Readers get a compact state portrait from the encyclopedia's early-twentieth-century vantage point, grounded in census figures and church statistics rather than booster praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sparta:
Sparta, the celebrated town of the Peloponnesus also called Lacedaemon, appears several times in the books of Maccabees. This entry examines its curious link with the Jews. Letters passed between the high priest Onias I and King Arius I about 309 or 300 before Christ. In them Arius claimed a document proving Spartans and Jews were brothers, both descended from Abraham.

Arius, seeking allies against Syria's successors of Alexander, had reason to invent such kinship. The entry judges the claim weakly founded, though some tradition may lie behind it. Later Jonathan renewed the friendship by letter, and the entry follows that diplomacy, giving Bible readers a window onto how small states used ancient ancestry as statecraft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anastasius:
St. Anastasius Sinaita was a Greek church writer, born at Alexandria in the first half of the seventh century and dead after 700, who earned the nickname the new Moses. This entry follows the abbot of Mount Sinai's monastery, so fierce an opponent of Monophysites, Monothelites. And Jews that the name stuck, and his chief work, the Hodegos, or Guide, defended the Catholic faith against those heretics as a popular manual of controversy among medieval Greeks.

His Questions and Answers on theological matters, 154 in number, are partly spurious. While his Devout Introduction to the Hexaemeron ran to twelve books, of which only the first eleven survive, in Latin translation. The entry lists his writings in Migne and notes Le Quien's unsupported attribution of another work to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-attracta:
St. Attracta, or St. Araght, was a contemporary of St. Patrick, from whom she received the veil. This entry follows a foundress of several churches in Galway and Sligo in Ireland. Colgan's account of her life rests on one written by Augustine Magraidin in the last years of the fourteenth century, and it abounds in improbable statements. Yet the fact that Attracta received the veil from Patrick is corroborated by Tirechan in the Book of Armagh.

The passage in the Documenta de S. Patricio records that Patrick placed a church in the cell of Adrachta, daughter of Talain, and that she took the pallium from Patrick's hand. A native of County Sligo, she resolved to devote herself to God. Opposed by her parents, she fled to South Connacht and made her first foundation at Drumconnell near Boyle in Roscommon, before moving to Greagraighe, or Coolavin, in Sligo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eata:
Eata, second bishop of Hexham, spent his working life redrawing the map of the northern English church. A disciple of Aidan, of English or Pictish birth, he was elected abbot of Melrose as early as 651. When Northumbria grew too wide for one see, Archbishop Theodore split off Bernicia in 678 and made Eata its bishop. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 26 October 686.

His new diocese held two seats, Hexham and Lindisfarne, at opposite ends of Northumberland. The arrangement lasted only three years: Hexham passed to Trumbert, and Eata kept Lindisfarne. After Trumbert's death, Cuthbert was elected in 684. The entry is a compact lesson in how early dioceses were carved, joined, and rearranged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eusebius-o:
Eusebius of Samosata, bishop in Syria until 379 or 380, held the Nicene line through the Arian storms of the Eastern church. Unknown before 361, he first appears consecrating Meletius, newly elected patriarch of Antioch, whom Arians backed in the belief he shared their views. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 notes some historians thought Eusebius himself then leaned Arian.

Whatever his earlier leanings, at Antioch's synod of 363 he signed the Nicene formula with its word homoousios, alongside twenty-four other bishops. When Arians found Meletius orthodox, they declared his election void and demanded the synodal acts entrusted to Eusebius. The entry follows a bishop guarding documents as firmly as doctrine, through deposition, exile, and return.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-godeberta:
Godeberta, virgin of Noyon, turned a court marriage debate into a vocation with a golden ring. Born about 640 at Boves near Amiens to noble, court-connected parents, she was carefully educated. When her marriage was discussed before King Clovis II, Eligius, bishop of Noyon, as if by inspiration, gave her a golden ring and hoped she might serve God. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Noyon to the early eighth century.

Moved, as the entry tells, by the Holy Spirit and sudden divine love, she refused brilliant prospects and noble suitors. Declaring herself Christ's spouse, she asked Eligius for the veil. Opposition soon melted, and she entered her new life under his guidance. Impressed, the Frankish king gave her a small palace, the seed of her community. The entry follows a ring, a refusal, and a royal gift.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ita:
Ita, called the Brigid of Munster, founded Killeedy and fostered saints, including Brendan the Voyager. Born in present County Waterford about 475, she became a nun at Cluain Credhail, ever since called Killeedy, Church of St. Ita, in County Limerick. Her austerities are told by Cuimin of Down, and many miracles are recorded of her. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 15 January 570.

Gifted with prophecy, she was held in great honour by many contemporary saints, men and women alike. Feeling her end near, she called her nuns and blessed clergy and laity around Killeedy. As foster-mother she raised Brendan the Voyager, Pulcherius, and Cummian Fada, among others. At Bishop Butler of Limerick's request, Pius IX granted a special Office and Mass for her 15 January feast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-zita:
Zita, model and heavenly patroness of domestic servants, served one Lucca family for decades with meek endurance. Born early in the thirteenth century to a poor family at Monsagrati near Lucca in Tuscany, she grew in sweetness, modesty, and conscientious work under a virtuous mother's teaching and divine grace. At twelve she went to work for the Fatinelli household of Lucca.

Her piety and exactness, regarding herself as serving God rather than man and covering fellow servants' failings, at first won her ill treatment from servants and, through their accusations, from employers. Incessant ill usage could not rob her of inward peace, love for her wrongdoers, or respect for her employers. By meek, humble restraint she finally overcame their malice. She died at Lucca on 27 April 1271, famed for miracles and bread for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-faustinus:
Faustinus and Jovita were brothers of a noble Brescia family, the elder a priest and the younger a deacon. This entry tells how their bold preaching brought them before the emperor Hadrian, who had them tormented at Brescia, then at Rome and Naples, before they were beheaded back at Brescia.

Bollandist dating puts the death in 120, while Allard argues for 118. Their many Acts are mostly legendary, and a recent Jesuit writer doubts nearly every detail in them. Only their existence and martyrdom stand firm, attested by early martyrologies and a lasting cult. Brescia still honours them as chief patrons, on 15 February.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-quiricus-:
Quiricus and Julitta were martyred under Diocletian, mother and infant son together. This entry follows their Acts and the early proof of their cult. Julitta fled Lycaonia with her three-month-old child when persecution broke out. Reaching Isauria and then Tarsus in Cilicia, she saw her boy killed before her eyes, and then she herself was put to death.

Veneration spread early in the West, shown by a chapel to them in Rome's Santa Maria Antiqua and by testimony from Gaul. Their relics are said to have reached the monastery of Saint-Amand in the diocese of Tournai. The feast is observed on 16 June, and the Constantinople Synaxarium sets it on 15 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-avesta:
Sacred books of the Parsees, or Zoroastrians, hold the focus here, as the chief source for the religion and inner life of ancient Persia. The collection stands in Iranian literature much as the Vedas stand in India. Its familiar label Zend-Avesta rests on a mistake, the entry warns, reversing the Pahlavi phrase Avistak u Zand, meaning text and commentary, since Zand denotes explanation rather than scripture itself.

Contents follow: hymns, laws, rituals, and later writings, with their languages and dates. Little reached Europe about Persian faith before the Avesta arrived in the eighteenth century, and the entry traces its discovery, translation, and scholarly study. For readers new to Zoroastrianism, it opens the door to a religion older than most of the world's great faiths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theological-a:
God in the Avesta, the holy books of the Parsees, is the theme of this entry on Zoroastrian belief. Ahura Mazda, the All-Wise Lord, stands as Supreme God, later called Auharmazd in Pahlavi and Ormuzd in modern Persian. Mazdeism takes its name from him. A pure spirit, he bears eternity, wisdom, truth, goodness, majesty, and power.

Creator of all good things, but not of evil, he rules as Lawgiver, rewarding good and punishing ill. He dwells in Eternal Light, and later books call light his clothing or body, a sign of his presence like the Shekinah of the Old Testament. Lists of his traits, omniscience, omnipotence, all-sovereignty, and all-goodness, crown him Supreme Sovereign, Wise Creator, and Supporter of the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tosephta:
The Tosephta, Hebrew for addition or supplement, is a compilation of legal and narrative teaching modelled on the Mishna. It belongs essentially to the era of the Tannaim, the early rabbinic teachers, and lacks only four Mishna tractates: Aboth, Tamid, Middoth and Qinnim. Its editors drew on sources older than our Mishna.

Its legal rulings show less subtlety and precision than the Mishna, and the course of discussion often lets the reader trace how a ruling grew. Narrative teaching is also fully present. How the work arose is still unclear, and in its present form it holds many doctrines of later rabbis, the Amoraim, so it was not edited until the late Talmudic period. Zuckermandel argued it preserves the Palestinian Mishna, re-edited in Babylonia as ours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trani-and-bar:
Trani and Barletta form a united diocese in Italy, on the Adriatic in a fertile plain yielding grain, wine and oil for export. Trani's Byzantine cathedral, built by Canon Nicola in 1143, keeps bronze gates by Barisano from that age. Outside the city stands the old abbey of Santa Maria de Colonna with its mineral spring, the water of Christ.

Built on ancient Turenum, Trani grew under Byzantium, fell to Saracens in 840 and 1009, and lived as a republic under nominal Byzantine rule. Its Ordinamenta et Consuetudo Maris of 1063 is the second oldest maritime code of the Middle Ages, after Amalfi's tables. Trani resisted the Normans until 1073, fought Roger of Sicily at Bigano in 1137, and later joined Barletta, whose see of Nazareth united with Trani in 1860. The united dioceses hold nineteen parishes and 98,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wichita:

At its founding it held sixteen priests in charge of churches, twenty-three churches served as missions, nine parochial schools. About eight thousand Catholics, but no religious communities.

In 1897 the Holy See added fourteen counties east of the sixth meridian, extending the eastern boundary to Missouri's western line and continuing Indian Territory's northern line southward. Its first bishop, James O'Reilly of Topeka, died in July 1887 before consecration, and a year later John Joseph Hennessy was chosen and consecrated at St Louis in November 1888. dutt-manu-samhita:
Dutt's English Manu Samhita appeared in 1909, late in his translating career. The Laws of Manu form ancient India's great code of duty. No legal text has shaped Hindu custom more deeply over time.

The code sets out caste duties, marriage, food, and rules for kings. Penance, gifts, and the stages of life get the same firm order. It also teaches the soul's path through duty toward final release. Scholars use the text to grasp classical India's social frame. Dutt's version keeps the famed code open to plain English readers today. Charles Ives, the composer and insurance executive, wrote these essays as a preface to his piano sonata. The sonata, named for Concord, Massachusetts, portrays four figures of Transcendentalism in music. Transcendentalism was a New England movement stressing spirit, nature, and self-trust. He jokes that essays serve readers who cannot stand his music, and music serves those who cannot stand his essays.

A prologue asks what music can carry: substance, the idea, versus manner, the dress. Essays take up Emerson the philosopher-poet and Hawthorne the novelist of guilt and dreams. The Alcotts chapter evokes Bronson Alcott's talk and his daughter Louisa May's household world. Thoreau closes the set, with Walden Pond, flute playing, and self-reliance as themes. An epilogue returns to the question of how much of a life music can hold. Musicians read the book as Ives explaining himself; readers read it as a composer's tribute.
europe-and-the-faith-sine-auctoritate-nu: Europe and the Faith, Sine Auctoritate Nulla Vita, Hilaire Belloc's Catholic history. The faith's Europe. This book preserves that history. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
gjellerup-der-pilger-kamanita:
Karl Gjellerup set his novel of ancient India in the days of the Buddha, and German readers meet it here as Der Pilger Kamanita. Kamanita, a merchant's son, leaves wealth and comfort behind. His road leads toward a teaching that promises release from pain and desire.

Along the way, love, loss, and chance meetings test the young pilgrim's resolve. Gjellerup, who shared the Nobel Prize in 1917, writes with calm and grace. East and West meet in the tale, since a Danish author retells an Indian quest. Readers find a serene story of the search for truth and inner peace.
govdocs-archive_org-mda-mdma-and-other-m:

MDMA appears in the files decades before it became a street drug, and later a therapy candidate. The paper is a documented chapter of psychopharmacology's secret history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LorenzMarita_Lo:
Vanity Fair published 'The Spy Who Loved Castro' in November 1993, a profile of Marita Lorenz. Lorenz had been a lover of Fidel Castro as a young woman. She later claimed knowledge of plots around the Kennedy assassination, and her story pulled her into that debate for decades.

The profile appeared thirty years after Dallas, when magazines were revisiting the case for the anniversary. Lorenz's life crossed the era's main currents: Castro's Cuba, exile politics, intelligence work, and courtroom testimony. The piece presents her as she presented herself, a woman who said she had stood close to famous events. Readers can weigh her claims against the record she never quite settled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MilitaryAssista: The Department of State Bulletin reprinted this statement by Secretary of State Dean Rusk under the title 'International Defense Commitments of the United States.' govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MusgroveRita_Mu:
A writer signing himself 'Fred' sent this letter to 'Ed' on July 8, 1974. The two men were exchanging assassination literature among the critics of the official account. Fred mentions William Turner's piece in Ramparts magazine. He also encloses a column by Mike Royko, the Chicago columnist.

At the letter's end, Fred states his own conclusion: President Kennedy's life was taken by a small conspiracy. The letter is a sample of how the research community actually worked. Books and articles moved by mail between men who mostly knew each other by post. Along with the clippings went judgments, argued in the margins, like the one this letter closes with.
govdocs-archive_org-strike-of-the-russia: The Strike of the Russian Gods attacks world religions from a pagan point of view. It also charges those religions with mind control over their followers. The library holds the book as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. Its value for study lies in its stance: a modern pagan writer turning the language of exposure against the faiths that replaced his own gods.
la-fiammetta:
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote La Fiammetta, translated here by James C. Brogan in 1907. Its prologue calls it the elegy of Madonna Fiammetta. She sends her tale to ladies in love.

Fiammetta speaks in her own voice about her sorrows in love. She hopes her pain will win pity from happier women. She does not want her words to reach the ears of men. The book stands as an early, intense portrait of a woman abandoned by her lover. Her grief unfolds as a long, direct address to women readers. Few early books give a woman's sorrow this much space.
lucasta:
Lucasta gathers the poems of Richard Lovelace, the Cavalier poet. The first part holds poems addressed to Lucasta herself. Songs tell of going beyond the seas and going to the wars. There are odes to a rose, a dialogue, and Lucasta weeping.

One famous piece is 'To Lucasta, from Prison,' an epode of defiance. Lovelace fought for King Charles in the Civil War and knew prison. His verses mix love, honor, and a soldier's swagger. 'Stone walls do not a prison make' is his best-known boast. Lucasta herself was the lady who inspired his finest songs. The poems shine with the grace of the Cavalier age.
mary-gusta:

Marcellus had lived in Ostable for fifty nine years, much talked of. The girl had drawn scant thought while he lived. Lincoln opens with a young news man at work on the death notice, and with a town keen to guess. Even the death notice shows Lincoln's dry Cape Cod humor. Big questions in town start, here, from one small girl's fate.
nasa-tm-19630006262-the-effects-of-wing-:
Stuart L. Treon of Ames Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-364, in April 1960. It asks how wing shape affects a flat-top hypersonic aircraft. Plan form means the wing's outline as seen from above. Tests ran from Mach 0.6 to 1.4, through the sound barrier.

Treon measured pitch stability traits for each wing outline. A craft built for hypersonic speed must also fly at slow speeds. Its wing choice shapes balance in both regimes at once. Small outline changes can shift lift and upset trim. This study gave designers a fair test of rival wing plans for the flat-top craft then on drawing boards.
nasa-tm-19650019839-wing-sweep-and-blunt:

Tests ran in helium tunnels, which can reach such extreme speeds. Their subject was how wing sweep and leading edge blunting change a delta planform's behavior at that speed.

At Mach twenty, a vehicle is in the hypersonic range of reentry flight. Small shape choices have large effects on lift, drag, and heating. The paper sets out the terms and measures used, then reports the effects found. Designers of very fast vehicles used such tunnel results to choose wing shapes with more confidence.

nasa-tm-19670009441-dual-frequency-20-0-:
Chesley H. Looney Jr., of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, compiled this data report in January 1967. It presents a year of very low frequency radio measurements at two close frequencies, 20.0 and 19.9 kilohertz. Such signals travel inside the ionosphere, so their timing shifts carry information about conditions overhead, including effects tied to solar activity.

Both signals came from station WWVL, each locked to the National Bureau of Standards master clock within a microsecond. Goddard received them with Tracor receivers referenced to a cesium-beam frequency standard, itself checked against hydrogen masers. Twelve tables give daily phase angle measurements, corrected using bureau data. The dual-frequency record, Looney explains, resolves a timing ambiguity inherent in the single 20.0 kilohertz signal, pinning the transmitted phase difference down tightly.

The observations rest heavily on photographic plates, including Palomar plates whose locations are charted. Anderson was the center's acquisition scientist, and Niksch its technical editor. The note announces that Apollo 14 pictures are available for study. obiter-dicta:
Augustine Birrell titled his essays Obiter Dicta, a law term he defines up front. An obiter dictum, says an old judge, is a gratuitous opinion, an individual impertinence. Wise or foolish, right or wrong, it binds none, not even the lips that utter it. Birrell dates his preface to the American edition February 13, 1885.

That preface calls the book a very little one to introduce to so large a continent. Scribner proposed the edition, and Birrell found being read in America delightful. Contents treat Carlyle, the alleged obscurity of Browning's poetry, and truth hunting. Actors, a rogue's memoirs, the via media, and Falstaff complete the list.
on-limitations-to-the-use-of-some-anthro:
John Wesley Powell wrote this paper for the Smithsonian Institution. Powell directed the Bureau of Ethnology at that time. He warns that archaeology findings are often misused. Workers had linked American tribes to ancient Old World races. Powell calls such uses of the data illegitimate.

He reviews mounds, graves, ruins, and scattered works of art. Such finds can show how art grew in early life, he says. They may hint at customs of their makers. But they cannot prove grand racial links abroad. He notes man's wide spread by very early times. The paper urges care and limits in science.
overland-through-asia-pictures-of-siberi:
Thomas Wallace Knox traveled overland through Asia in the 1860s. He published his Pictures of Siberian, Chinese, and Tartar Life at Hartford in 1871. Agents sold it by subscription only. Nearly two hundred illustrations and a map fill it. The full title promises travels in Kamchatka, Siberia, China, and Mongolia. Full accounts of the Siberian exiles come with them. Their treatment, condition, and mode of life are all described. The Amoor River and the frozen ocean's shores close the promise.

His preface notes that in fourteen years only one other book, Major Collins's Voyage Down the Amoor, had covered the ground. Knox crossed the Russian empire when the route was sleigh, boat, and horse. His sketches of exile colonies and river peoples made the book a standard American account of Siberia.
podcast-joerogan-J3Wqw8Az7TA:
Author Gregg Braden joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2387. Braden writes and lectures on human potential, arguing that people carry abilities that modern life teaches them to ignore. His books blend science claims with spiritual teaching, and they have found a large audience.

He lays out his case for Rogan: that the heart, the body, and old traditions hold knowledge science is only now measuring. Rogan asks where the proof is strong and where it is faith. The episode gives Braden's worldview a full, friendly hearing, and listeners can judge how much of it they buy.

Weinstein explains why he thinks academia punishes bold ideas and protects its gatekeepers. He outlines his theory in broad strokes and the cold shoulder it received. Rogan asks how a smart outsider should judge such claims. Theory fans get a window into a feud between one mind and a whole field.
sacred-books-east-vol-10-dhammapada-sutt:
Volume ten of the Sacred Books of the East, issued in 1881, joins two of the oldest Buddhist texts: the Dhammapada and the Sutta-Nipata. F. Max Müller translated both from the Pali. Müller edited the whole Sacred Books series at Oxford, which carried Asia's scriptures to English readers.

The Dhammapada holds 423 short verses on the mind, anger, craving, and the path to release. Its lines are the best-known words of Buddhism in the West. The Sutta-Nipata is older and rawer: poems of wandering monks, snakes, and fierce self-reliance. Together they give the Buddha's teaching in its most direct, quotable form.

Butler charges that Romanes cited a Canon Kingsley piece on instinct from a journal that did not yet exist at the date given. He notes that he asked in print for the true source and got no answer. Wit and grievance mix here, as Butler defends his own views on memory passed from parent to young.
seraphita:
Honore de Balzac wrote this mystical tale, here in English by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Balzac inscribed the work to Madame Eveline de Hanska, who had asked him for it. He calls it a sketch of a figure dreamed of since childhood, drawn from the depths of mystic thought.

The tale opens on the wild coast of Norway, beneath strange northern skies. A being named Seraphitus stands at its heart, loved and wondered at by those nearby. Balzac blends love story with Swedenborg-style teaching on spirit and heaven. The book closes his studies of faith with a strange, glowing vision of the soul's ascent.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States built from talks with former slaves, was typed from records made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume II, the Arkansas Narratives, Part I. Its list of those who spoke begins with Silas Abbott, Lucian Abernathy, Laura Adeline, Aunt Adway, Rose Aiken, and Liddie Aldridge.
texas-a-brief-account-of-the-origin-prog:
Texas, a brief account of the rise and state of the colonial settlements of Texas, came out in 1836 as a short pamphlet pulled from a larger work then near press. Some parts had run first in the New Orleans Bee and Bulletin.

Its preface warns that war fills the day, so only a slice of the source work's public case is given here. The writer argues that Texas settlers were forced into war with Mexico by steady abuse and breach of rights. Their fight, he says, seeks freedom and sound rule, not gain or conquest. Readers get a wartime plea for the Texas cause, made in the year of the revolt itself.
the-great-north-western-conspiracy-in-al:
I. Winslow Ayer wrote The Great North-Western Conspiracy in All Its Startling Details. Ayer was a doctor of medicine. His long title page lists the matter: the plot to plunder and burn Chicago, free rebel prisoners, and seize arsenals. It promises raids from Canada, a plot to burn New York, and piracy on the Lakes. Portraits of leading characters go with the text.

His introduction takes up the trial before the Military Commission in Cincinnati. That trial, he says, drew out testimony of the most startling kind. It showed a deep, well-arranged conspiracy, favored in the great cities of six states. But for timely discovery, he argues, it would have ended in disaster. He credits a merciful Providence for the country's escape. The book is his full account of the plot and its trial.
the-inca-of-perusalem-an-almost-historic:
George Bernard Shaw called this wartime playlet an almost historical comedietta. His preface insists on when he wrote it. The central figure was still a feared foe then. The Caesar of the piece was no fallen prisoner. Many readers could not forgive Shaw's laughter. Laughing at a deadly peril seemed heartless. Anyone doubting German skill in war risked a hard name. Such doubters were called pro-German.

The fighting has since shown the Inca was doomed. Shaw now faces the opposite charge. Critics may say he hits a man when he is down. He reports cutting any foul blows from the proofs. The play first reached an English stage in 1917. The Pioneer Players performed it at the Criterion Theatre. Its prologue opens with an English archdeacon. He comes through the curtains in extreme irritation.
the-jew-of-malta: Marlowe's fierce 1590 tragedy about Barabas, the rich Jew of Malta, who answers Christian persecution with spectacular revenge. Bloody, blackly comic, and deliberately shocking, it gave the Elizabethan stage one of its great villains. The play's portrait of greed and hatred still provokes, and its verse still thunders.
the-life-of-the-truly-eminent-and-learne:
M. de Burigny wrote his life of Hugo Grotius in French, and this English edition appeared in London in 1754. His preface wishes that so celebrated a genius had found a historian equal to his fame. Earlier writers, he says, gave only surface accounts of the life plus catalogues of the works.

Burigny promises a full history of Grotius important negotiations and a critical account of his writings. He praises Lehman defense of Grotius memory as fuller than the rest. Charles Butler later life of Grotius, held elsewhere in this library, drew heavily on Burigny work.
the-magna-carta:
Magna Carta itself, the great charter of 1215, is the text held here, in a file whose preparer's note admits that some versions arrived a little mangled in transit. The charter opens in King John's own voice. John, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, greets his archbishops and bishops. Abbots, earls, barons, and officials are greeted too. John states that the grant is made for the health of his soul and his ancestors' and heirs'.

He acts on the advice of named churchmen and barons, from Archbishop Stephen of Canterbury to William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke. Its first clause grants that the English Church shall be free, with its rights undiminished, for the king and his heirs in perpetuity. Readers meet the famous document directly, in its own formal language.
the-mansion-of-mystery-being-a-certain-c:
Chester K. Steele's The Mansion of Mystery, published in 1911 by the International Fiction Library, presents itself as a case taken from the note-book of Adam Adams, investigator and detective. Chapter one, The Story of a Double Tragedy, opens with a young man in a tremendous hurry. First ashore from the ferryboat, he leaps into a taxicab and orders the driver to take him to the Vanderslip Building with all possible speed.

In the cab he buries his chin in his hands. His handsome face is wrinkled with care, his hair disheveled, and he looks as if he has lost much sleep. "To think that she is guilty!" he mutters, shaking as if with fever, and twice starts up to check whether he has arrived. Steele opens his detective tale on a client's anguish before the investigator even appears.
the-naturalist-in-la-plata:
W. H. Hudson's The Naturalist in La Plata, in a third edition published in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1895, carries illustrations by J. Smit. Hudson, joint author of Argentine Ornithology, explains his plan in a preface. He sifted and arranged facts about the habits of the animals he knew best, keeping only what seemed worth recording, and grouped linked subjects under single headings.

Much of the material first appeared as papers in the Field and other natural history journals, and in magazines such as Longman's and The Nineteenth Century, whose editors allowed reuse. Hudson apologises for an unoriginal title in the line of The Naturalist on the Amazons. Birds, he notes, gave him most pleasure, though most of his fresh bird knowledge sits in his earlier book.
the-outdoor-girls-on-pine-island-or-a-ca: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls on Pine Island, or A Cave and What It Contained, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists show Pine Island as the seventh Outdoor Girls volume, after Ocean View. Hope's Moving Picture Girls series, from Oak Farm to At Sea, and her Bobbsey Twins books fill the remaining space, at 50 cents a volume.
the-story-of-malta: Maturin M. Ballou's history of Malta, dated 1893, is presented here through its opening publisher's pages alone. Those pages list Ballou's other travel books. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published them. Equatorial America and Aztec Land stand among them. A summer journey to Alaska follows. Volumes of travels due west, south, and north come next. Then the title page of the Malta volume begins. Ballou's account of the island itself does not appear.
the-suppression-of-the-african-slave-tra: Volume one of a Harvard Historical Studies monograph appeared in 1896. Longmans, Green, and Company published it. It treats the suppression of the African slave-trade to the United States, 1638 to 1870. No author's name is printed here. Only the title page and a detailed contents opening appear here. An introductory chapter gives the plan of the work and the rise of the English slave-trade. Chapters on restrictions follow. They treat the planting colonies of Georgia and the Carolinas. Virginia and Maryland come next. The history itself does not appear.
the-uttermost-farthing-a-savant-s-vendet:
R. Austin Freeman subtitles his Uttermost Farthing A Savant's Vendetta, sharing a title and motto idea with a very different novel. The narrator publishes, with misgivings, the strange history confided by his late friend Humphrey Challoner. Challoner's ethical standards, he warns, stand far from ordinary ones and may repel readers.

Challoner was a great savant spoiled by untimely wealth, once noted as a comparative anatomist and criminal anthropologist. When known to the narrator he seemed a mere collector, endlessly adding specimens to a private museum. Later revelations changed that picture. Contents chapters promise a motive force, numbered victims, gifts of chance, and a serpent's trail, marking the story as methodical revenge.
the-valley-of-vision-a-book-of-romance-a:
Henry Van Dyke calls The Valley of Vision a book of romance and some half-told tales, dedicating it to his children and grandchildren. His preface answers a friend who asked why a valley, not a mountaintop, should give the widest view. Van Dyke replies that the mountaintop overlooks earth and sea, but the deepest visions of life's meaning come in valleys.

Suffering, endurance, and self-sacrifice are the valley's teachers in his account. He reads the recent world war as a victory over Germany's peak-born illusion of world dominion, won by Allied strength grown through valley visions of right and justice. The tales themselves are fables and fantasies, sketches grave and gay, where more is meant than meets the ear.
un-doc-declaration-of-alma-ata:
The Declaration of Alma-Ata came out of the International Conference on Primary Health Care. World Health Organization and UNICEF backing brought the meeting to Alma-Ata in September 1978. Health gaps between rich and poor lands were wide and growing. The delegates sought a fairer base for care.

Health, the text says, is full physical, mental, and social well-being. It is a basic human right, not a prize for the few. The goal set was health for all by the year 2000. Basic care near home is the key: clean water, food, shots, mother and child care, and vital drugs. Local people must help plan and run that care.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Specific Problems with Personal Data forms part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Police work now means gathering and linking files on named people. That power sits uneasily next to privacy. Each land draws the line in a different place.

The survey points to one landmark court ruling. West Germany's top court held that state storage of personal facts can chill free action. A clear law must back each such file, the court said. Some newer state charters name data privacy outright. In most lands, though, the rules sit in mixed spots: trial codes, data acts, or police laws. Hard limits on police files stay rare.
vendetta:
Honore de Balzac wrote Vendetta, rendered into English by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. He dedicated it to Puttinati, a sculptor of Milan. Chapter one, a prologue, opens in the year 1800, late in October. The scene stands before the palace of the Tuileries in Paris. A foreigner waits for a long time near a house just pulled down. A woman and a little girl wait with him.

The man folds his arms and bows his head. Then he lifts it, to look from the palace to his wife. She plays with the child's long black hair, yet misses none of his glances. Balzac says some bond other than love ties them, and names it: misery. Misery, he adds, is perhaps the strongest of all ties. The stranger's broad head and black hair streaked with white mark a proud Corsican exile. The tale builds toward the feud of its title.
woodroffe-shakti-and-shakta:
John Woodroffe, a Calcutta judge, wrote Shakti and Shakta in 1918 as Arthur Avalon. His book gives the classic English account of Tantric Shaktism. The worship of the Divine Mother stands at its warm center.

Woodroffe treats the Goddess as the world's living power and soul. He explains her rites, mantras, and images with a scholar's care. His sympathy for a faith mocked by many set the work apart. Western readers met Tantra as deep thought, not mere scandal, here. The book launched the modern study of Tantra in English for good. Its chapters still serve as the first door into Shakta thought.
